Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in debate on Bill C-62, an act respecting telecommunications.
Bill C-62 proposes sweeping changes to the framework surrounding the telecommunications industry. Those changes reflect the Conservative government's insistence to deregulate and privatize wherever conceivable. We saw these kinds of things taking place when the Liberals were in government and tried to deregulate the airlines. I can remember going to those committees with our member from Regina and telling the government, the Liberals at that time, that it was the wrong thing to do. However, they persisted and we now see what has happened to the airlines because of the deregulations that took place then.
There is no doubt in the New Democratic Party's mind that this is another deregulation step because of the free trade agreements made with the United States. It is the patent drug legislation all over again, making it accessible for others to compete in Canadian markets.
While my colleagues and I have called for an updated telecommunications act to drive Canada into the 21st century, this is not the right vehicle. Canada's telecommunications industry generated $21 billion in revenue last year. It employs 125,000 people.
I will argue that this bill should not be passed at second reading for four main reasons. I understand that again the Liberals are prepared to go along with the government.
The first reason is very simple. According to Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second reading is the most important stage through which the bill is required to pass for its whole principle is then at issue and is affirmed or denied by a vote of the House. According to the Minister of Communications this bill will undergo substantial amendments during the committee stage.
April 19, 1993

At one time the Department of Communications was asked to redraft this bill to take into account the substantial amendments recommended by the Senate transport committee which engaged in a pre-study of this bill. The minister alluded to that during his speech.
It is clearly not correct for this House to pass a bill in principle which will be altered fundamentally at committee stage. Government members may argue that the principle of this bill remains unchanged, but this bill contains seven sweeping policy objectives. Changing any of these policy objectives would undeniably alter the principle of the bill.
The Senate committee recommended changes to those policy objectives. How can any member of this House pass a piece of legislation in principle when the true form of the legislation will not be clear until the amendments are made? Yet that is what the Liberals have said they are prepared to do. They will follow along with the government's proposals.
The second reason this bill should not be passed is clear to anyone who pays a phone bill. In June 1992 the CRTC decided to open up the long distance market. It accepted Unitel's application and assertion that long distance competition would not cost consumers more. If this deregulation experiment fails, the CRTC's hands will be tied. Under this legislation every decision the CRTC makes must diminish regulation and at every turn increase competition.
According to what this government says, the more deregulation we have, the more Canadian consumers will benefit. According to the CRTC local rates would not increase as a result of long distance competition. Yet less than a year ago, after the CRTC decision, telephone companies across this country applied to the CRTC for rate increases left, right and centre.
The telephone companies are asking for these increases for one simple reason. The name of that is cross-subsidization and it is what has put our Canadian telephone system leagues ahead of foreign competitors.
Government Orders
Before the CRTC's June decision every long distance telephone call made by a consumer, small business or multinational corporation cross-subsidized local rates. I hope if this bill does go to committee that the minister will ensure that some pensioners will be able to come to that committee and express their concerns of what could happen to their rates and to their very vital, important communication with other groups. Our long distance rates were higher than they had to be, but for a reason. That was to offset the cost associated with local telephone services.
Local telephone services in Ottawa, Vancouver or Calgary can cost the telephone companies up to 10 times less than providing service to remote locations such as in northern and rural areas. Yet people living in those areas are not paying 10 times more than people living in Toronto, Vancouver or Calgary. It is because of crosssubsidization, which is what has made 92 per cent of Canadians say that they are happy with the telephone service.
Cross-subsidization has given more Canadians phone than in almost any other country in the world. Ninety-eight per cent of Canadians have a telephone. That is a higher penetration rate than in the United States and most European countries.
Bell Canada recently applied to the CRTC for a rate increase. If its application is accepted, local rates will jump as much as 65 per cent.
BC Tel has also asked for a substantial rate increase as well. It wants not only the recent rate increase in its local rates, but also increases in directory assistance, charges and service calls.
Alberta Government Telephones has applied for a 30 per cent increase on its local rates. Ron Liepert from Alberta Government Telephones said in February of this year: "Long distance rates have decreased by 40 per cent". This action means that the proposed 30 per cent increase in local rates is the other side of it.
Both BC Tel and Bell want to charge more for service calls and for directory assistance. These proposed increases all fly in the face of the government's continuing insistence that deregulation and competition will bring rates down.

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
Two separate reports have indicated that charges for local calls have increased world-wide when governments have accepted to reduce long distance rates through competition.
According to the Brussels based European Consumers Organization the gap in the cost of service is widening between small and large users in most nations.
This report that was released in early 1992 said that Canada is one of the most successful models of competition. It is important to note that this report was completed before the CRTC announced its decision to deregulate the long distance market and before this bill was passed.
It is obvious that we used to do things right. According to this report, countries that introduced competition the earliest have the largest gap in cost between small and large users.
A conclusion must be drawn that competition does not help consumers or small businesses. According to the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development, before long distance competition was introduced in Canada, our businesses paid less for their local calls than businesses in the U.S., France, Italy, Belgium, West Germany, Austria and Britain.
Again, before long distance competition was introduced, long distance rates for calls within Canada were 15 per cent below that of the OECD average. Prices for international business calls were 17 per cent lower than the OECD average.
The government's own briefing document which discussed the effects that long distance competition was likely to have states: "Competition will require gradual decreases in cross-subsidization and therefore increased rates. This will hit residential and small business users hardest while big business users will benefit". That is exactly the point we are trying to make. We do recognize that for many people in the outer areas the costs are greater and that the big users across the country should help subsidize those areas to ensure that they are available to them. However, the government seems to turn a blind eye to that.
This is according to the same government that keeps on spinning the same tired line that deregulation is going to save consumers money. We can rest assured that it is not going to save money for the average consumer in the small, remote areas.
In the same briefing document the Department of Communications quoted a Peat Marwick study that suggested that local rate increases over five years of between 13 per cent and 93 per cent would be required on a year-by-year basis. This represents 2 per cent to 12 per cent per annum. These increases correspond quite nicely with the increases requested by BC Tel and Bell.
Again, according to the government's document, the annual drop-off rate due to such changes could amount to 2,500 to 7,500 subscribers across Canada.
The chapter goes much further and limits the terms and conditions that Canada will be able to impose in the future. Specifically, legislators will be required to ensure that prices charged for telephone services are based on the economic costs directly related to providing such services.
Although NAFTA will allow cross-subsidization between our existing telephone companies to continue, we will not be able to require resellers to make the contribution payments that are necessary to support universal service. Again, this falls right in line with the government's free trade agreements.
This bill does nothing to prevent this erosion of cross-subsidization.. This bill actually encourages deregulation regardless of its effects on consumers and small businesses in Canada. There is no compassion for our seniors, many of whom cannot get out of their homes and the telephone is their vehicle by which they can communicate with their families. There is no compassion whatsoever.
Again I say to the minister that I hope seniors will be allowed to come to this committee to have their voices heard.
I have with me an advertisement from AT&T in The Wall Street Journal that says: "In 1993 this border will no longer be a barrier". The border they are talking about is the Canada-U.S. border.
This bill prevents foreign companies from owning more than 20 per cent of the telephone company. We think that this provision should have been put into legislation a long time ago.
The problem is that this provision is the only protection Canadian telephone companies are going to get with this legislation. The bill opens the door to resellers and AT&T could be considered a reseller under this legislation. AT&T has enough excess capacity to simply swallow all of Canada's telephone businesses within a hiccup.

In the United States, long distance service is subsidized by local rates. High local rates and local measured services are a fact of life for many Americans. That is why many Americans need telephone welfare or subsidized telephone service to be able to afford a telephone. That is the kind of service this legislation would bring us closer to.
Another reason that this bill should not be supported at second reading is that this bill as it stands now jeopardizes the arm's length relationship between the government and the CRTC. Not only does the legislation eliminate any semblance of independence between the CRTC and the government, this bill also makes a mockery of the process of public hearings.
This bill puts a collar around the neck of the CRTC and hands the leash to the government through regulations. Not only will the government have the power to review the CRTC's decisions but the Governor in Council will be able to direct the CRTC on broad policy measures. The Governor in Council will be able to exempt any class of carrier from the regulations contained in the act. We in this party are not prepared to give that kind of authority to government.
This bill will make the CRTC no more than an advisory body to the Governor in Council rather than an independent watch-dog of public interest. During the pre-study of this bill, the Senate committee noted that forbearance lies at the heart of Bill C-62. Indeed it does.
This government shamelessly promotes competition simply for competition's sake. This bill will ensure that the CRTC has no choice but to follow the government's lead. If this bill is passed, consumers will be at the whim of an industry trying to maximize its profits. The public will be put once again on the back burner.
Look at what is taking place right now regarding some of the things that have happened because of decisions that were made. On April 15 Alberta Government Telephones, AGT, announced over 1,000 job cuts. The president, Don Lowry, said that the job cuts to be phased in over nine months are largely in response to the bid by Unitel Communications to compete in the lucrative long distance market.
Government Orders
Look at the job cuts in BC Tel. Brian Canfield, president of BC Tel, announced on April 16 that his company was working to reduce staff size by 4 per cent this year through incentives. BC Tel has already seen 422 employees accept voluntary separation packages. BC Tel earned $205.7 million last year, which is up $2.3 million from the year before.
Mr. Canfield said: "The entry into the Canadian market of U.S. phone giant AT&T which bought 20 per cent of Unitel after the CRTC last year approved Unitel's entry into the long distance field added weight to BC Tel's argument that inflated long distance rates should not be used to subsidize artificially low rates".
There we have the kinds of things that are already taking place in the telecommunications industry. If we allow this government to proceed with this piece of legislation in its present form or with the procedures that it is trying to follow through deregulation and competition, then only the people of Canada will suffer.
This is especially so in the remote areas where people with their ordinary telephones are trying to communicate with each other. They will be the big losers. The big multinational corporations that this government seems to want to support to bring about these kinds of changes would get ahead.
Also, this would give the government the authority to override the one very historic area that it has had: the CRTC. The CRTC was an independent group. As much as we may have seen the weaknesses in it, it was a group that would hear submissions, make decisions and bring them forward.
We will not have that if this piece of legislation is passed. We are opposed to this legislation. We will do everything we can to ensure that proper and adequate witnesses are brought before the committee and their views are heard.

Mr. Speaker, I was not quite prepared to intervene at this point but I will certainly take this opportunity to say a few words regarding Bill C-62, a bill dealing with the telecommunications industry in the Canadian economy.

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
We are dealing today with an aspect of the Canadian economy that has been on the cutting edge of change and dynamic development for many years. We have been world leaders in a variety of areas of telecommunications. It has been a Canadian growth industry and continues to be a growth industry. It is a great employer. The telecommunications industry directly employs 125,000 people in our country and accounts for up to 8.6 per cent of our GDP after inflation.
Change in terms of its legislative mandate has been in the offing for many years and for many years we have called for a modem day approach to the development of telecommunications, recognizing that our telecommunications industry is currently governed by the antiquated Railway Act. We have called for the government to change this.
Over the years we have heard various ministers give their views on what the change ought to be. Today we are beginning a discussion on Bill C-62, which is this government's effort to fill the policy vacuum when it comes to the very dynamic field of telecommunications.
To say this is long overdue is not really selling the point very adequately because subsequent ministers have been promising this action. I want to at least acknowledge that the present minister of telecommunications has actually brought forward legislation. It was first introduced in the spring of 1992, many months ago. Now we are beginning the debate at second reading as this session of Parliament begins to essentially wind down in anticipation of the general election.
This legislation takes the telecommunications sector and places it on the sacred altar of privatization and deregulation. We have seen a number of other sectors placed on this altar for sacrifice such as the trucking business in Canada a few years ago. The feeling was that if we deregulated and privatized the trucking industry we would see a dynamic sector emerge. Jobs would be created and the Canadian trucking companies would prosper and benefit.
At that time a lot of us had contrary views. Many people in the trucking industry had contrary views and wondered how a deregulated environment that was being proposed, as well as the privatization that occurred
in the transportation sector generally would be helpful. The result has been that literally hundreds of Canadian trucking companies have gone bankrupt over the last number of years and tens of thousands of drivers and others associated with the industry have lost their jobs. It has become a much less competitive industry.
The airline industry is one of the more recent sacrifices on the altar of privatization and deregulation. Once again it was proposed that a deregulated environment would result in increased competition, better service to the consumer and reduced fares and rates. The result is that an airline has just announced in the last few hours that it is going out of business because it is bankrupt. The two major carriers in Canada are in bankruptcy stages of one kind or another and unable to compete in this deregulated environment.
If I can use my own community of Kamloops as an example, two airlines are now competing head to head for service. This was welcome news because we thought it would result in a greater variety of services and an abundance of departure times to Vancouver. The result is that two aircraft fly into the Kamloops airport at the same time and leave for the same city at the same time.
There is head to head competition but no increased opportunities for travellers and we have seen the rates increase month after month. Any citizens who wish to fly from Kamloops to Vancouver or Calgary should forget about it unless they are independently wealthy or have some kind of business expense account. No one can afford the kinds of rates the airlines are now charging in this new competitive environment.
The Minister of Communications is saying the telecommunications sector is our new sacrifice to lay upon the altar. Who will benefit from this? Surely someone must benefit.
My colleague for Kootenay East has made an excellent presentation as to why he feels this initiative is inappropriate. On many occasions I have listened to my colleague for Okanagan-Shuswap explain to anyone who would listen why this initiative is not in the best interest of Canadians. One has to ask who will benefit from this.
April 19, 1993

I think it is fair to say that Canadians generally will not benefit but some large transnational telecommunications company will. AT&T will eventually be one of the main beneficiaries of this initiative. Those companies that are now prepared to come in and cream off a very lucrative long distance market will be the beneficiaries.
The average Canadian and the average small business operator in Canada will be the losers. I want to explain why that is the case but before doing that I would like to read a few figures into the record. We are not leaders in this matter of telephone and telecommunications deregulation. Other countries have done this before us and we need look no further than the United States.
Some of the leading political voices in the United States said a number of years ago it would benefit the average American if they deregulated the telephone industry, which they did, but the average consumer did not benefit from this initiative.
In the United States, residential telephone rates have doubled in some cases and tripled, quadrupled or increased five times in others. I will give an example as of today and use my own community because it will vary somewhat across the country.
In Kamloops, the basic residential rate for telephone use is $10.05 per month. Naturally, the cost of other services is added to that amount. In other communities it is less. I know in Thunder Bay where there is a private telephone company, the rates are less than $8 per month. We have enjoyed a regulated environment in Canada for many years and we are viewed world-wide as having one of the more sophisticated telephone systems found anywhere.
Recent surveys have found that 92 per cent of Canadians are very satisfied with their telephone service. This goes back to the old adage: If it ain't broke, don't fix it. If there is a 92 per cent satisfaction rate with just about anything in the country today, I think it would probably be a good indication to just keep our hands off and stay out of it. Obviously the regulated telecommunications telephone business in Canada has been working very well and 92 per cent is not bad.
Obviously the government has decided to work on behalf of somebody in our society to change this. Let us
Government Orders
make some comparisons. The Kamloops basic rate per month is $10.05. Let me just randomly pick out a number of American centres. In Jacksonville, Alabama they pay $43.48 a month; in Phoenix, Arizona, they pay $24.36; in Little Rock, Arkansas they pay $32.01 and in Denver, Colorado they pay $32.39 a month. In Wilmington, Delaware, they pay $22.30 a month; Fort Lauderdale, Florida, $29.10 a month; Twin Falls, Idaho, $28.56 a month. Here is a good one, in Indianapolis, Indiana, they pay $47.40 a month; in Sioux City, Iowa, they pay $36.60 a month; in Louisville, Kentucky, they pay $47.76 a month.
I think you get the idea, Mr. Speaker. I have a list here of dozens and dozens of communities from a small survey that was done to get some idea of what has happened in American communities as a result of deregulation. I think it is fair to predict that a few years from now the people of Kamloops will not be paying a rate of $10.05 a month. They will be probably paying $34 a month as in Tulsa, Oklahoma, or $37 a month as in Eugene, Oregon. That is the reality.
Let us be clear what we are doing here. The government has opened the door to allow companies to ask for rate increases so the average consumer in this country, the average small business operator in Canada will see their rates double, triple or quadruple over the next number of years. That is the obvious direction we are taking.
In the Wall Street Journal a little while ago there was a full page ad by AT&T, the big multinational telecommunications company, which included a map. The ad said: "Here's a map of North America with a border presently between Canada and the United States". As soon as this legislation goes through we can take an eraser and erase this border because Canada and the United States are going to be simply one happy integrated area as far as AT&T is concerned. In other words this is another way of describing the free trade agreement.
Now the North American free trade agreement is accompanying this legislation, Bill C-62, through Parliament. They are going side by side in a parallel process through Parliament. We know that the NAFTA agreement includes Mexico.

Government Orders
Let me make another projection. Not too many months from now when we dial the operator to get information or dial the telephone company to check out the nature of our bill, the person responding will say something like Buenos dias, senor, because that operator will be operating out of northern Mexico. After all, if a telephone operator in Canada is paid $16 an hour and the same operator with the same skills is paid 60 cents an hour in the Maquiladora zone in Mexico, why on earth would an unregulated company not simply take advantage of the lowest labour costs possible?

We oppose this legislation to say the least. We, as New Democrats, have long felt, as many ministers over the years have suggested, that the way to develop our telecommunications industry, create world technological leadership in this sector and be on the leading edge of change, growth and dynamic development is through a regulated sector of telecommunications. In other words, there must be sophisticated, progressive, updated regulation of this very critical sector. That is the way to proceed and not what we see in Bill C-62.
There are many reasons why we do not want to proceed at this point with Bill C-62 at this second reading stage. Second reading stage is when we talk about and debate the principle of the bill and whether or not we want to proceed even with the principle that is being discussed and introduced here in the House of Commons. The Minister of Communications and his staff have been very generous in being straightforward
with the people of Canada because they have indicated that this bill will undergo substantial amendments during the committee stage. The work of the other place points out a whole number of shortfalls so the minister has been very generous in his comments and said that, yes, major changes must occur.

Therefore the process is open to some question. We believe that the minister should be a bit more forthright in explaining just what it is the government plans to change and to what extent it plans to alter the provisions of this legislation.
The other reason that we oppose this-I rather tangentially referred to it earlier-is the fact that this will result in significant rate increases for Canadians.
I wonder if this is the time when the Government of Canada should be passing legislation that it knows will result in additional costs to Canadian consumers and Canadian citizens generally at a time of a call for restraint, when governments are calling for cutbacks in budgets and when governments are calling for all Canadians to tighten their belts. A lot of Canadians do not even have a belt left any more. They have tightened them so many times there are no notches left.
The government comes along and says: "At a time when we are calling for cuts, restraint and thought in terms of the small business person, we are introducing legislation that is going to definitely result in cost increases". It seems that the minister has not been privy to discussions concerning what one hand is doing or saying obviously because here with this initiative we will see additional costs for the consumer.
There are other reasons why we oppose this legislation. My colleague from Kootenay East explained in some detail the value of cross-subsidization. The charges for the users in those areas of Canada where the intensity of telephone use is very high help offset the cost to the more rural or small town user. In other words, in order for people to have relatively similar access to
April 19, 1993

telephones, there is cross-subsidization so that the heavy users subsidize those where the costs are increased.
This has served Canada well. We are the second largest country in the world geographically. We are spread out between three major coasts. We have one of the highest rates of telephone usage in the world. One of the reasons is that people living in the small towns and rural areas of Canada were subsidized by those living in the urban areas or the more urban corridors of communication within our regulated environment for so many years. This has served our country well. However, this will no longer be the case as a result of this legislation. That principle is being eroded here and that is another reason why we oppose it.
You have given me a signal, Mr. Speaker, indicating that my time is now limited. I simply want to conclude by saying that traditionally we have had in Canada an excellent telephone system. We have an excellent history in terms of the development of telecommunications. It has served us well. Ninety-two per cent of Canadians like the present system. I think many of us have had many reasons to be proud of the developments within our telecommunications sector for many years. We have hard-working men and women in this sector. There are tens of thousands of them who would like to keep their jobs and continue serving Canadians in this particular profession and line of work.
For that reason we will oppose this legislation when it comes to a vote and encourage the Minister of Communications, the minister responsible for this particular legislation, to take this back to his caucus and cabinet colleagues. He should say that this is not the time to increase rates across the country or to introduce legislation that would result in job losses to so many more Canadians, but that this is to be set on the back burner permanently.

Mr. Speaker, this certainly is a bill whose time has come. Unfortunately it is also a bill that is quite seriously flawed.
The previous speaker for the New Democrats stated unequivocally that they will be voting against the bill. While I understand that, I say that from our point of view we believe the bill must go to committee where it can be
Government Orders
reviewed and substantially amended to reflect the needs both of industry and of the people of Canada.
This bill has taken rather a long time from its own introduction well over a year ago by the hon. minister or from the first statement from this government in 1984 when the then Minister of Finance, in an economic statement, said there was a clear need for national telecommunications to take advantage of opportunities presented by a rapidly changing technology and a demand for Canadians for new telecommunication services. As I said, it has been nine years since that statement. The phrase labouring and bringing forth a mouse comes to mind because in nine years this bill is the best the government has been able to come up with. This bill, as already stated by my colleague from Mount Royal, is seriously flawed. Consequently, in our party we are prepared to allow the bill to go to committee at this stage. However, I say in the wake of the member for Mount Royal that we serve notice that we expect to see major amendments in committee.
Bill C-62 would establish in law a Canadian telecommunications policy, extend the regulatory authority of the CRTC to provincial Crown corporations and provide new powers with respect to the regulation of telecommunications. It is designed to give the force of law to a Canadian telecommunication policy, consolidate and modernize existing statutes and respond to the Supreme Court of Canada's decision in the Alberta Government Telephones Act with regard to the AGT clause.
It is necessary, of course, to put forward some regulation in today's ever changing telecommunications industry. Telecommunication industries employ over 100,000 Canadians and generate over $20 billion in revenue. In essence, this industry is one of Canada's key links to the globalization of markets and the world of high technology. It is, of course, also an area in which Canadians can be justly proud of the developments that are homegrown in Canada.
I am reminded of a visit last year that the Subcommittee on the Status of Women made to the United States when we were doing our study on breast cancer. We were visiting the Office of Women's Health in Washington and a conference was set up with the Centre For Disease Control in Atlanta. It was a teleconference. There was a

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
large television set at one end of a boardroom table where we could see the people from Atlanta and there was a similar set-up in Atlanta. After the meeting was over, one of the Americans said to me: "How do you like our technology?" I noted the Northern Telecom logo on the television set and I said: "You will have to excuse me, but in actual fact that is our technology". I think it was something that all of us there felt very happy about.
However, it is not enough to rest on our laurels in the area of telecommunications. The industry and Canadians deserve the best bill available. They deserve the best law that reflects what the industry needs and what the population needs. This is not happening.
We support the bill's attempt at unifying a national jurisdiction over telecommunications. A new and stronger piece of legislation would affirm the essential role that telecommunications must have in the maintenance of Canada's identify and sovereignty. These things are only sensible. They are so self-evident that they almost go without saying. However, I have learned in over four years in this place that very little tends to go without saying. It affirms Canada's commitment to the industry as well as the industry's role to provide a world class product and service to Canadians.
I will get into the specifics of this bill. Clause 2 attempts to define the various players or carriers and transmission facilities in the telecommunications industry. My party and the Senate pre-study report, which was presented in June 1992, believe that more consideration should be given to these definitions to clear up any ambiguities. One such example is how a common carrier, or one that relies on a Canadian carrier, should be dealt with.
The CRTC submitted this during the Senate hearings: "The ambiguity in the definition must be removed by clearly setting out what is meant to be included and excluded".
Clause 14 of the bill makes it necessary for the federal government to consult with the provincial government when a decision "would have a substantial impact on a Canadian carrier that was the principal telecommunications carrier in that province". This clause of the bill must not allow either level of government sufficient
power to paralyse an effective telecommunications policy.
Part II of the bill makes provisions to establish the criteria a Canadian carrier must meet in order to be eligible to hold a licence to operate. Any policy direction taken by the federal government with respect to this must again ensure that it contains a strong commitment to the telecommunications industry's future. In its commitment to the telecommunications industry's future, it must ensure that it is a Canadian future.
Under this proposal the communications minister would have the power to decide who will be licensed. My party does not agree that the minister should create for himself as many new powers as he does in this clause. This move essentially adds further steps to the regulatory process and would in effect slow the process down. There is also no requirement for the minister to give reasons for licensing decisions. Far be it from me to suggest that the current minister would ever make such a decision without giving the best, clearest and most well-explained reasons at any given time. Here I am complimenting him all over the place and he is not even listening. However, I think that the requirement for reasons in licensing decisions is absolutely essential.
Part III of Bill C-62 would establish the framework with which the CRTC would be authorized to regulate the telecommunications services offered by a Canadian carrier. One of the main powers assigned to the CRTC by the bill is that of forbearance. The CRTC would be able to exercise forbearance only after it had determined that a sufficient degree of competition existed to protect the user's interests.
Again, in my party we want to make sure that this new power does not result in the deregulation of our telecommunications industry. Now that competition among carriers is on the increase it must be recognized that the consumer must not end up the loser or bear unnecessary inflated charges.
Clause 46 of Bill C-62 allows the CRTC to prohibit or regulate any type of unsolicited telecommunications, unsolicited telephone calls and faxes. The key object of this clause must be to recognize that telemarketing companies have a right to do business while at the same time protecting Canadians from unwanted phone calls.
April 19, 1993

Clause 46 does not go far enough to reconcile these two conflicting points. The key objective of any comprehensive telecommunications policy should be reliability, affordability, quality and accessibility for all regions of this country.
I put emphasis on the question of accessibility because accessibility and level of service in the telecommunications industry is something of which Canadians can be justly proud. It is also something upon which Canadians depend and depend upon very strongly.
Every one of us in this Chamber knows that we are unlike almost any other country in the world because of our huge geography and small population. The telecommunications industry probably more so than almost anywhere else on earth is a true lifeline for literally hundreds of thousands of Canadians.
It is essential and will remain essential to the country's development, yet it has taken the government over nine years to finally act. The nine years of labouring has not brought forth the kind of a bill that makes anyone in this House want to stand up and cheer. I suppose a few of the people on the other side want to stand up and cheer but I have not seen them do it.
We in the Liberal Party want to make sure there are no more delays in the establishment of a national telecommunications policy and in the legislation to build it up, but it must be the right legislation.
This bill needs revision and further clarification. It is too open ended and too ambiguous in many of its sections. It needs fundamental revision. For example, clause 14 makes it necessary for the federal government to consult with the provincial government when a decision would have a substantial impact on a Canadian carrier that was the principal telecommunications carrier in that province. The difficulty is that the bill is not strong enough to prevent one level of government possibly paralysing an effective policy.
The difficulty is that in the history of federal and provincial relations, the possibility of this taking place is not particularly far-fetched.
In establishing a policy of telecommunications, we are
Government Orders
all aware that certain expectations have been set and that there are certain areas in which Canadians have such a vested interest that to leave them with a bill that is too broad and too ambiguous does the kind of disservice that we just do not need to put up with.
As I said before, we support this bill going to committee but at the same time we want assurances that changes are planned. Virtually every person in the telecommunications industry that has made a comment has said these changes are necessary. Since the bill was introduced, these changes have not been forthcoming.
We have had problems with the fact that the minister and the government delayed the bill for well over a year. It was the government that delayed the bill, not the opposition. The minister has had the opportunity to build agreement on a national level and he has not done so. Various and sundry other projects and reports have been done and been available but no action has been taken on them.
Consequently in the time since this bill was first introduced in February 1992, we feel that a lot of time has been wasted and a lot of water has gone over the dam which could have been used in making it a better mix and a better reflection of what both the industry and the people of Canada would like to see in a national telecommunications policy. A bill which could do that would have been good for the industry, good for business and good for Canadians as a whole.
We are not talking about delay. Indeed the opposition has not in any way attempted to delay the bill. If anything, we have been urging from the sidelines faster and better policy development in this area. Had we wanted to delay it, given this government's fondness for the use of closure, the best we would have been able to do would be to pipe dream a delay. That is not the response here.
The telecommunications industry is a serious and important industry to the make-up of this country. We are not going to sit here as Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition and give approval to something which we think is inferior.

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
We believe that the parliamentary process can create something better. We on this side of the House, led by the hon. member for Mount Royal as our senior critic, are prepared to do everything we can to ensure this bill is the best it can be. We would like to hear from the government and most particularly from the minister that it is the intention of the government to clear up some of these problems. In the 14 months since the bill was first introduced, we have waited in vain for some small indication that this was going to be the response of the government. It has not happened.
Again I say we are serving notice that in committee we will be seeking these amendments. I cannot say or else because unfortunately the system is such that we do not have an or else. I think in the interests of the country and in the interests of the telecommunications industry it is the very least we can expect from the government.
The telecommunication industry is vital to the way this country works. It is vital in the employment of tens of thousands of Canadians. It is vital in the revenues in the billions that it generates. It is clearly a strategic industry for the Canadian economy. It is clearly part and parcel of the new Canadian identity as we face a globalized economy and as we face competition in international markets.
We are entering the age of communication as we are told by experts in all fields on any given day at any given time. Therefore, it is even more essential we not walk into this new age of telecommunications covered with the shreds of inferior legislation. What we need is the best legislation that the Government of Canada can produce for the industry and for the people.
I will close by saying this. The telecommunications industry is so much a part of what makes Canada the country it is and what will make Canada the country it can be that we on this side of the House serve notice to the minister and the government that we will be coming to committee prepared to battle down to the wire for
every one of the amendments we believe to be utterly crucial.
I expect to be there holding the coat of the member for Mount Royal who is a formidable opponent in these matters. She will be our major spokesperson. I can only say that if these amendments do not pass, if these amendments are not brought into law, if the government does not see that its bill is flawed and makes it better legislation for Canadians, then the sorrow will be not just to the industry and the people of Canada, it will be very much to the sorrow of the members of this House.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. It being two o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 30, the House will now proceed to Statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 31.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has an onerous task ahead of him as he completes his budget. He is to be commended for the
extensive pre-budget consultation that he has held across Canada.
It is a major challenge to reduce and eliminate our deficit. The problem is not just ours within this Chamber, all Canadians must share the challenge of balancing our wants with our needs and both of those with our ability to pay. If we learned nothing else from last year's referendum we should have learned that Canadians think for themselves and want to be involved in decisions that affect them.
With this in mind I invited the people in my constituency to offer suggestions on the budget and they responded. In a random but extensive survey they told me that they want restraint and no tax increase. I was told that transfers for health care, education and seniors' pensions are too important to be reduced, while regional development, special interest groups, unemployment insurance, Crown corporations and even farm aid need to be re-evaluated.
I have a strong message from Red Deer, one that tells me Canadians are ready to accept the tough decisions that must be made.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week, three separate reports showed how severely the Montreal region has been affected by the recession.
First, according to Statistics Canada, Montreal has now set a new record, with more than 22 per cent of its citizens living below the poverty line. Second, a report by the World Health Organization states that the living conditions of street children in Montreal are similar to those in the Third World. As if that were not enough, a study by a committee that included experts from the city of Montreal indicates that 40 per cent of the city's thousands of homeless people are under 18.
In a statement about the intolerable situation in this country today, the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops said that society's moral fibre was undermined as a result of the Conservative economic policies of the past 10 years.
No matter who wins at the leadership convention, Canadians will massively reject the Conservatives who are responsible for all this suffering.

April 19, 1993
[English)

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 30 years ago this spring John F. Kennedy was President of the United States, Harold Macmillan was Prime Minister of Great Britain, John Diefenbaker was Prime Minister of Canada and the Toronto Maple Leafs won the Stanley Cup.
I would like to bring to the attention of this House that yesterday marked the 30th anniversary of the first election of the Leader of the Opposition to this House. I am sure all members will join me in congratulating him on his many years of service to his party and to our country.
During those years this hon. gentleman has held many high offices, none higher than the one he holds today. There is one higher that has eluded him. Alas, my sense of history tells me it will continue to elude him. I must tell you, Mr. Speaker, I am a great prognosticator so you should listen to that point.
Nevertheless, as we approach the election that will, I suspect, mark the twilight of his career I invite all hon. members to join me in paying tribute to the leader of the Liberal Party on this auspicious anniversary.

Mr. Speaker, taking barley sales to the United States out of Wheat Board jurisdiction is a return to the bad old days of grain marketing. A Conservative-Liberal union government created the first single-desk Wheat Board during World War I largely to save grain traders who had sold more paper than there was wheat. Farmers quickly learned the benefits of single-desk selling but the government took that privilege away for another 15 years until a dying Conservative government introduced a voluntary board in 1935.
The voluntary board clearly did not work and was made compulsory in the early 1940s for wheat, oats and barley. I know the Minister of Agriculture and the Conservative Party have never liked single-desk selling.
To even consider taking barley sales to the U.S. away from the board demonstrates that. When I see the government deliberately undermining Wheat Board marketing power, which means lower barley prices to farmers, I can no longer believe the government's protestations of support for the Wheat Board, supply management or farmers. Its actions speak louder than its words.

Mr. Speaker, in 1991, a trilateral agreement was reached on an integrated management plan for renewable resources, covering forestry and wildlife in an area of about 10,000 square kilometres, partly located in the La Verendrye wildlife reserve and surrounding area in Quebec.
The Barrire Lake Algonquins were proud of the work done by all parties to this agreement and, personally, I see it as a good example of how they and both levels of government were able to co-operate to ensure that aboriginal people can look forward to a better future and do so within the context of a new relationship.
Today, the Algonquins have former Liberal Environment Minister Clifford Lincoln as their negotiator. On April 16 Mr. Lincoln said this went beyond the question of logging operations in La Verendiye Park. Now the First Nations are involved.
What a fuss about a 20 or 60 metre strip of forest.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBIanc (Cape Breton Highlands - Canso):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, where is the minister of fisheries hiding? For months he has been promising that by April there would be a federal compensation package to support communities in eastern Nova Scotia devastated by last December's quota cuts. April is more than half over and there has still been no announcement.
April 19, 1993

A task force from the Nova Scotia government proposed a plan to him a month ago. Now not even his Nova Scotia counterpart, Mr. Legere, can get him on the line.
Yesterday more than 200 fishermen and plant workers gathered once again at a public meeting in Canso to call for an end to this uncertainty. Their patience is wearing thin. Fishermen need to know whether there is any point in putting their boats in the water. Plant workers need to know what the future holds for them. They want the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to come to Canso and explain what his government has in store for them.
The minister knows what needs to go into this plan. Will he end the uncertainty gnawing away at this community and at so many other communities in Atlantic Canada so they can get on with their lives?

Mr. Speaker, the beauty and fragrance of fresh flowers have returned to Niagara regional council chambers. More than 200 plants and cut flowers filled the chambers for the introduction of the Greater Niagara Greenhouse Growers' Directory and Buyer's Guide, a Niagara Region Development Corporation project.
The industry employs almost 2,200 people working under more than 11 million square feet of glass and generates multimillion dollar amounts of revenue. Niagara greenhouses grow 17 species of cut flowers. In addition, growers are recognized for their excellence in producing millions of poinsettias, vegetables, nursery stock and landscaping plants. Major markets include the Niagara region, southern Ontario, Quebec and the northeastern United States. Annual sales are $160 million.
Seven Niagara greenhouse growers have been in business for more than 50 years and two-thirds have been growing in Niagara for more than 20 years. Congratulations to the growers in Niagara.

Mr. Speaker, April 19 serves as a testimony to bravery in the face of barbarism and the triumph of the human spirit over mass
oppression, starvation, disease and the evil perpetrated by the Nazi movement.
The Warsaw ghetto uprising took place 50 years ago and today we recognize the heroic members of the Jewish resistance who rose up in defiance of cruel tyranny. Jewish resistance fighters, with support from the Polish underground, fought a desperate battle with no hope of winning. This tragic revolt is a reminder that we must never again tolerate regimes based on racism or ethnic cleansing.
In honour of those who died in the Warsaw ghetto I call upon the international community to oppose institutionalized oppression in all its forms, regardless of race, religion or ethnocultural background.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to this week, April 18 to 24, as it is National Volunteer Week.
This is an opportunity for all of us to express thanks and to join communities across Canada in giving recognition to the more than 13 million Canadians who volunteer their time, skills and energies. Volunteers have become an essential and vital part of Canadian society and a major economic resource.
Volunteers often fill gaps by performing indispensable tasks that would not otherwise be done. Organizations, such as hospitals, libraries, schools, food banks, community associations, and a whole variety of both domestic and internationally concerned organizations, would all suffer greatly without this volunteer support. The average volunteer devotes 191 hours a year to volunteer work. Altogether Canadians give more than one billion hours of their time to voluntary organizations. The collective value of volunteer time is more than $13 billion a year.
It is appropriate for us to say thank you to everyone who works for or supports a volunteer organization. Through their work volunteers build a more caring and compassionate Canada. Their generosity assures that many organizations, programs and activities continue because without volunteers' commitment they would falter or cease to exist.

April 19, 1993

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a new tour that is going to occur shortly. It is called the "Hire Me, Here is My C.V. Tour" of the Prime Minister. Guess who will foot the bill for this tour? You are right, Mr. Speaker, it will be Canadian taxpayers again.
In 1991 the Canadian taxpayer sponsored the Asian tour at a cost of $1 million, or $80,000 a day. This new tour is going to be at bargain basement prices. It will cost only $50,000 a day.
Tour organizers are said to be working hard to improve the show of the advance performance in Florida last week because the Prime Minister did not meet expectations when he met Mickey Mouse.
Canadians are sure glad to know our present Prime Minister is finally on the way out and they will not have to sponsor tours again because rumour has it that the next tour would have been named the "Fly Me To the Moon Tour", in honour of the spaced out colleagues in his caucus who are seeking the Tory leadership.

Mr. Speaker, my constituents have made it clear that they see government deficits as the major issue for all levels of government to address.
Recently, several provincial governments have announced measures to reduce expenditures. These steps are similar to those taken by the federal government over the past number of years.
Based on comments I have received throughout Wild Rose, the federal government must continue on a path of fiscal responsibility to become even leaner and more efficient.

Mr. Speaker, more than a tonne and a half of persistent toxic chemicals daily enter Lake Ontario including more than a tonne of lead, 400 kilograms of arsenic and more than a kilogram of PCBs.
For the Niagara River it is no longer adequate just to study how to cut toxic contaminants in half by 1996. Action is needed. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has introduced tough regulations aimed at protecting human health and the ecosystem. Unfortunately there is little progress on Canada's side.
Two years ago the agreement between Ottawa and Ontario to implement the water quality agreement expired. The government has not renegotiated this agreement. We urge this government to conclude negotiations on a new federal-provincial agreement respecting Great Lakes water quality. This is the minimum required to match action with rhetoric.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to remind the House that April is dental health month.
Good dental health is important for our well-being and our looks. Bad teeth and gums affect our ability to eat properly and lower our self-esteem. We know that we must see a dentist every six months, but do we really know everything that must be done to keep our teeth in good health?
During dental health month, the Canadian Dental Association and its provincial chapters will help us increase our knowledge of dental health with exhibits in shopping centres and other health promotion activities.
So please join me in wishing the Canadian Dental Association and the provincial dental associations a very successful dental health month.

Mr. Speaker, on April 19, 1943 Nazi forces entered the Warsaw ghetto to kill or remove all of its occupants. Rather than surrendering the Jews in the ghetto rose up against the Nazi forces determined to fight the inevitable for as long as they could. After 27 days the uprising was crushed. Most of

the ghetto's 60,000 people were killed and the few

Hear, hear, thousand that survived were sent to death camps.
Fifty years later the Warsaw ghetto uprising and the heroism of the men, women and children who stood up against the attacking Nazis remains as an unforgettable example of human courage in the face of unspeakable evil. It was only one event in the nightmare of the Holocaust which saw the murder of six million Jews. The Warsaw uprising continues to serve as a powerful reminder of that systematic, terrible slaughter.
In commemorating the Warsaw uprising we must reaffirm our commitment to human rights. This 50th anniversary must not only be a time to remember but must also be a call to action. We must translate "never again" into concrete anti-racist action. We must redouble our efforts to fight racism and anti-Semitism in Canada and wherever it occurs throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, on Good Friday in Victoria I was honoured to take part in welcome home ceremonies for the Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry returning from peacekeeping duties in Croatia. Local residents are extremely proud of the work our peacekeeping forces do abroad.
Yesterday 135 Canadian soldiers received a hero's welcome in the war-torn city of Srebrenica. Canada's peacekeeping forces in Bosnia have entered the besieged city to evacuate injured Muslims and disarm the government garrison.
Our hearts are with these brave soldiers working amidt a tenuous ceasefire in this bitter conflict. While the ceasefire holds in Srebrenica, the fighting continues unabated elsewhere in Bosnia. Once again Canada's peacekeeping forces are front and centre on the world stage doing their best to protect and save lives.
I know all members of the House will join me in wishing our peacekeepers a safe and secure return to Canada at the end of their tour of duty. We are proud of the work they do on behalf of us all.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance, I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question.
Last week, the Minister of Finance published a document announcing for the 10th or 12th time that the government's priority was to reduce the deficit, when we know very well that, for the last nine years, the government has run up deficits of over $30 billion a year on average.
In presenting the budget in the next few days, does the government intend to cut a $5.8 billion program to buy helicopters for the cold war with the Soviet Union when the Soviet Union no longer exists? Will the government accept the opposition's opinion and not buy these helicopters?

Mr. Speaker, the minister did release a document that talks about economic policy in a world of change and about the deficit.
We know that under our friends, the deficit started from nearly zero and grew to $38.5 billion, an increase of 300 per cent. Under this government, it has been cut in half, in terms of the gross national product, and has remained at $30 billion or $32 billion, but that is still too high. We have made very substantial progress in reducing the deficit and we did so by reducing the increase in program spending. Over a 15-year period, program spending had risen 13.8 per cent a year on average. This was reduced to 4.1 per cent over eight years and it is now 2.8 per cent. This is a spectacular turnaround.
Hopefully, this will continue with the finance minister's new budget, the deficit will eventually be eliminated and there will be a reasonable and effective approach to maintaining and reducing the national debt. That will not happen tomorrow but we are now going in the right direction.

April 19, 1993
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has refused to answer the question concerning helicopters.
I would like to point out the Minister of National Defence last week said that if one asks the Department of National Defence, it will give programs it will cancel first before cancelling the program for helicopters.

When will the government act on these programs, if they exist, to ensure that the Department of National Defence or other departments are not spending money like drunken sailors?
If anybody knows about that it is you.

With regard to the expenditures of the defence department, we have had the debate-

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Again the Prime Minister is evading the question. I asked him a very simple question.
Last week the Minister of National Defence said that she might reduce the number of helicopters from 50 to a lower number. A month ago she said that we should not cut one of these helicopters.
I want to know from the government when it will scrap this program. We do not need it at all. It is $5.8 billion of waste. We need the money to cut the deficit or do something to create some growth in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the things that this project does is create 45,000 person-years of employment in Canada in an area of high technology.
I would point out to the hon. Leader of the Opposition that the Department of National Defence has had its budget cut by $12 billion since 1989. Clearly the government has set priorities in expenditures and the Department of National Defence has cut back.
It is also important to point out that the choice is not between spending this money on the helicopters and zero; it is between spending this money on helicopters of 1990 technology for Canadian men and women in the services and throwing away $2.5 billion to extend the life of 40-year old helicopters after which time, five or ten years at the maximum, we would have to face the question of replacing them.
If that is Liberal economics, Mr. Speaker, I do not think we want any on this side of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister.
His Minister of National Defence has said she can eliminate the deficit in five years. His Minister of the Environment has said he can do it in only four years. I want to ask the Prime Minister who does he agree with, the Minister of National Defence or the Minister of the Environment? The job creation is worrisome here as it is in the United States. In the United States they are referring to it as a jobless recovery. Jobs are being created but the number of people entering the work force continues to exceed that.
All industrialized countries are concerned by it, which is the result of enhanced productivity, greater investment in people and in equipment and therefore the capacity to sell products internationally. It is a double-edged sword that is before us and that we are working with very closely, which explains the programs by the Minister of Employment and Immigration to create new jobs in that sector while allowing the private sector based on exports to do the principal element of work in creating new jobs.

I asked that question on behalf of a number of Canadians who had approached our offices on this issue. As a member of Parliament, I took the information that was given to me, which was false, and forwarded it to other Canadians.

I have a ruling which I am now prepared to share with the House on the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River regarding the tabling of Order in Council PC 1992-2715, pursuant to Section 59(5) of the Customs Thriff; and the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre regarding the tabling of the government response to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade report.
Members will remember that when the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre raised the matter, which he did, I advised him that a similar matter was before me and I would try to deal with them both at the same time.
I would like to advise all hon. members that I am now ready to rule on the question of privilege raised on Wednesday, February 24 by the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River regarding the failure of the Minister of Finance to table an Order in Council pursuant to section 59(5) of the Customs Thriff.
Regrettably this issue is not new to this House, having been raised by the hon. member just over a year ago. I would like to thank the hon. member for bringing this matter to the attention of the House again and the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance for the response.
I will deal as well in this ruling with the question of privilege raised on March 29, 1993 by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre concerning the late tabling of a government response to a committee report from the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade.
April 19, 1993

In presenting his claim for breach of privilege the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River explained that on December 29, 1992, pursuant to section 59(2) of the Customs Thriff, the Governor in Council adopted Order in Council 1992-2715.
The hon. member's question of privilege concerned section 59(5) of the Customs Tariff which explicitly states: "The Minister of Finance shall cause a copy of any order made pursuant to subsection 2 to be made before Parliament on any of the first 15 sitting days after the making thereof that either House of Parliament is sitting".
Pursuant to this statute, the order referred to by the hon. member should have been tabled on or before February 15, 1993. However as the hon. member noted, the Minister of Finance failed to do so.
For the information of all members I would like to note that the document cited was tabled subsequent to the question of privilege being raised on February 25, 1993. Nonetheless, this eventual tabling of the order does not correct the situation or resolve the fundamental problem.
Let me begin by saying that I find this situation particularly disheartening because of the striking resemblance it bears to the situation which gave rise to the question of privilege raised a year ago. In both cases the Minister of Finance was required by section 59(5) of the Customs Thriff to table an Order in Council within a prescribed time.
I am not making any of these comments in any personal sense and members will understand that but there are people in departments who know these rules and are supposed to ensure they are carried out.
In both of these cases the government failed to do so until after the matter was brought to the attention of this House.

The key element of the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River is based on a statutory requirement. That is, the ministry was legally obliged to table a copy of an order made by the Governor in Council within a time limit determined by the Customs Tariff.
Speaker's Ruling

I find it necessary to also repeat the hon. member's statement of one year ago that, and I quote the hon. member: "It is difficult to conceive of any command of this House that could have more legitimacy than one contained in a law passed by this House".
As the hon. member succinctly stated when this very issue was raised in February 1992: "Subsection 59(5) of the Customs Thriff is a statutory provision and statutes are the highest form of command that can be given by this House. In my view the disregard of that legislative command, even if unintentional, is an affront to the authority and dignity of Parliament as a whole and of this House in particular".

It is an opinion that I share and that I expect to prevail in this Chamber. The statutory laws which have been agreed to by members of this House do serve a purpose and are meant to be respected.

As a servant of the House of Commons it is my duty to uphold the dignity and authority of this place. It is an obligation of the Speaker with, of course, the support of the members. At the very beginning of a Parliament every speaker addresses the Crown as represented by the Governor General, by claiming all the rights and privileges, in particular that members may have freedom of speech in their debates, access to His Excellency's person at all seasonable times and that their proceedings may receive from his "Excellency the most favourable construction".
In the present case it is not merely an order of the House that has been violated, but a law duly assented to by the Crown as a constituent part of Parliament. The delegate of the Crown has not met the exigencies of the law of Parliament.
As I have said before, Canada is not an executive democracy nor an administrative democracy, but a parliamentary democracy. If the Speaker has to remind the Crown formally at the opening of every Parliament then those who serve it should take note.
As members are well aware, the tabling of documents constitutes a fundamental procedure of this House. It is a part of our rules and ensures that members have access to the information necessary to them to effectively deal with the issues before Parliament.

April 19, 1993
Tributes
In addition, as I mentioned a year ago, the rules of the House specify that all reports, returns and papers to be laid before the House in accordance with the requirements of the statute are automatically referred to a standing committee, pursuant to Standing Order 32(5). Consequently, ministers and departmental officials must ensure that required documents are tabled so the House has a copy for the information of members and for review by one of its committees.
The requirements contained in our rules and statutory laws have been agreed upon by this House and constitute an agreement which I think all of us realize must be respected.
There has been a growing number of complaints raised by members in the past year about responses to petitions not being filed within the required time and answers to written questions being answered late. I understand that we live in an imperfect world. Nonetheless, what I refer to is all on the record and today I am dealing yet again with a document not being tabled within the legally prescribed time period.
In addition, the member for Winnipeg South Centre raised the issue on March 29, 1993 that the government was in breach of Standing Order 109 by not presenting the comprehensive response to the report of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade on the future of Canadian military goods, production and export to the House within the 150 days required.

Members cannot function if they do not have access to the material they need for their work and if our rules are being ignored and even statutory instruments are being disregarded.

I believe the House management committee should be given the opportunity to look into this whole question of late tablings. I am therefore prepared to find a prima facie case of breach of privilege and allow the hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River to move a motion referring this matter to committee.
In this way I am allowing the House to decide whether or not it shares my concern about the growing severity of this problem. The House may then decide whether or
not it feels the House management committee should be tasked with considering the issue.
