I am very grateful that many hon. members have remained. Our colleague, Alex Patterson, who was well known to many of us in this place, and certainly well known to all of us from British Columbia, has passed on. This is our first chance since that happened to speak appropriately of Alex and give our proper sensitivities to his family. I am going to ask the hon. member for Fraser Valley East to commence.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour today to say a few words to note the passing of Alex Patterson, a former member of this House of Commons and my predecessor as the member of Parliament for Fraser Valley East.
Alex Patterson spent most of his adult life working on behalf of the people in Fraser Valley East. He represented the riding in Parliament for most of the period between 1953 and 1984. In that period he earned a reputation as a hard worker and served as an MP for both the Social Credit Party and the Progressive Conservative Party.
April 19, 1993

Alex generated a good reputation in the riding not based solely on his ties with the Social Credit Party or the PC Party but more as a hard working gentleman who emphasized being involved at the grass roots level in the community.
Alex Patterson was bom in 1911 in Raymore, Saskatchewan, a prairie boy like myself, and moved to Abbotsford in 1951. It was in the early years, while carrying out his responsibilities as a minister of the gospel in the Church of the Nazarene, that he was approached to run in the 1953 federal election. His background and training in the church gave Alex a very clear view of right and wrong. He tried to emphasize these positions in his speeches during his first election campaign and continued to do so as the member of Parliament.
Alex was first elected in 1953 and then defeated in the Diefenbaker sweep of 1958. He was re-elected in 1962 and was defeated in the Liberal victory of 1968. He was then asked to serve under the Progressive Conservative label instead of the Social Credit label and accepted that challenge. He was elected in 1972 and served in this House until 1984 when he announced his retirement and I was nominated to stand as the Progressive Conservative candidate.
It was my privilege to attend, along with my wife, the funeral services held in Abbotsford on April 6 and to express the condolences of my wife and myself to his wife Charlotte, their four children and their spouses and his many grandchildren who were there. They are a credit to Alex and Charlotte's life together. I want them to know that this House appreciates the contribution that Alex made not only to the community of Fraser Valley East in British Columbia but to Canada in his service in this House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Official Opposition it is an honour to pay tribute to our late colleague and friend, Dr. Alexander Bell Patterson.
There are many things that might be said about the former member for Fraser Valley, subsequently Fraser Valley East. Which member of this House, except for the member for Parry Sound, like Alex won fully nine of the eleven elections he contested over more than a 30-year period?
Tributes
In 1965 Alex was acting national leader of the Social Credit Party. In 1972 he changed parties and was elected again. As a friend, Ewald Rempel, noted the other day: "Regardless of what party he ran for he would have won. He was very popular".
People might dispute why he was so well loved. Having known him between 1979 and 1984 I think his success had much to do with his religious values and deep personal honesty. He saw elected office as a stewardship, an extension of the church ministry. He would never put himself ahead of his constituents. He cared about all of them without favour and without fear. He worked hard for farmers, small business people and all others in the Fraser Valley.
This is not to say that our colleague, while often low key, could not be blunt. Members will perhaps recall what he once said about the Trudeau government: "It has destroyed the confidence of the international community in Canada's economy. It has destroyed the confidence of Canadians". Similarly, he once described the CBC as: "One of the foremost purveyors of anti-social, anti-family, amoral philosophy, contributing to the undermining of the moral fibre of this nation". He was concerned with more important issues than political correctness. Pierre Trudeau campaigned twice during six months in Fraser Valley East before the 1974 election in an effort to beat him but Alex was re-elected.
I must not close without making reference to his beloved family, his wife Charlotte and his four children, Lawrence, Ruth, Goldie and Wayne.
In summary, Alex was a strong family man who both inspired and instilled traditional values and commitments to one's calling. The early years, when MPs were allowed one train trip for every three-month period, were often difficult but he was committed to doing the best job possible and working for the constituents of the Fraser Valley riding he represented for nearly 24 years.
Columnist Allan Fotheringham said prior to one election: "The Fraser Valley is definitely Patterson country". Community was important to him and he enjoyed the charity work carried out through his longtime association with the Kiwanis Club and the Chamber of Commerce. He was a good man who served full time in the Christian ministry for over 20 years before he was

April 19, 1993
Tributes
persuaded to run for Parliament. A colleague commented that his experience in the pulpit made him one of the easiest speakers to listen to in this House. Though his voice was strong and authoritative in the House his firm Christian faith was quiet and always consistent. His background in the ministry served him well in encouraging what he thought was the ethical fibre needed in parliamentarians.
When a secretary passed away and no funeral was planned several staffers asked Dr. Patterson to lead a memorial service for those who wished to remember and pay their respects. It was not unusual for colleagues and staffers from various areas of the Hill to drop by his office to discuss a difficult time or ask for a word of encouragement and advice.
Following a stroke in early March of this year our friend was in hospital for four weeks when family members were able to gather. He passed away peacefully in the arms of Charlotte, his loving wife of 56 years, with his children at his side. Alex is fondly remembered, deeply missed and will always remain so to his family, friends and colleagues here. He will remain a perfect example of a faithful husband and father.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues in the New Democratic caucus I would like to extend our condolences to Mr. Patterson's family and to join in remembering him and his service here in the House of Commons.
I remember him personally. We shared five years together here. Although I did not have the opportunity to work with him in committee and therefore did not get to know him very well the overriding image I have of him is that of a real gentleman. He was a fellow whom one could speak to in the elevator, the hallway or the House, and although members said he could be forthright he was the kind of person one felt one could talk to. Sometimes those things do go together. I want to express our condolences.
Looking over Mr. Patterson's career before I came to this House I noted that he was defeated twice and re-elected. That is not something that happens to a lot of members. It is an unusual thing for someone to be twice defeated at different intervals and then re-elected.
It shows his commitment to the House of Commons as a place where he wanted to live out his commitment to his understanding of reality.
I note also that he was a minister in the Nazarene Church and I appreciate that element of his vocation as well. Although as a fellow Christian I may have come to different conclusions about how we express our Christian faith in political life that is something I also want to take note of and to respect.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join my colleagues in paying tribute to a man everyone here respected. He was a man of whom it is easy to speak well because he was a good man. He was thought well of in the party, in the entire House of Commons and obviously by his constituents.
I remember my former colleague, the former member from Capilano, told me once that when Alex Patterson was speaking he would come down from his office and listen to him in the House. That says something about the quality of speaker that Alex Patterson was. It was good oratory but it was also good content. He was a good member of Parliament.
I think the members of the opposition also recognized that while he spoke in opposition he did not speak in malice. There is a great deal of difference between the two. We in the House of Commons need to learn lessons like that from a man like Alex Patterson.
Obviously he was also a good member for his constituency. As members who have spoken before me have noted, he was a man who was constantly re-elected. As my hon. friend from Winnipeg Transcona has mentioned, he could also be defeated but was re-elected. That does not happen too often.
He was re-elected under changing circumstances for his riding. If one compares the boundaries of his constituency in 1953 to what they were in 1984 one recognizes that there were many changes in his constituency both in its size and in its constituents. Yet he commanded the respect of the people all through those years. At the outset it was a constituency that was probably entirely

^I
April 19, 1993

agricultural and certainly rural. By the end of his career it was changing and becoming light industry and commercial. Certainly today that constituency is enjoying a different kind of change. Through those changing circumstances he always enjoyed the support and respect of his people.
I guess one could say that with Alex Patterson you could get old and maybe even old-fashioned, in the best way of interpreting that word, but he was never an old fogy. Old-fashioned in the best sense of the word, he maintained the values that have given Canada strength and made it the country that it is today.
We pay respect to him because he could be a pillar but he could also be pliable. That speaks well of him.
I want to join others in that respect. He was always in touch with the people. One could not be re-elected the way he was without being in touch with the people.
In the words of the book of Acts it was said that Barnabas was a good man. The same could be said of Alex Patterson.
I would like to add just one anecdote which does not come from his political career or the Chamber but his family life, which he has passed on to the next generation. He was a man of Scottish descent. As other members have noted, he was a minister in the Nazarene Church. One of his children went into the ministry and decided to go for further training in the United States south of the Mason-Dixon line. The grandchildren were put in public school in kindergarten.
On the first day home from school his grandchild came home all enthusiastic. He came home and said: "Mom, I have a terrific teacher. She looks just like you". The mother was pretty excited about this and could not wait for parent-teacher night to arrive so that she could see this teacher who looked just like her.
The night came and she went to visit the school to see her son's teacher, and she was black. Here is a teacher teaching a child who did not see the colour. That did not happen by accident. That was not a casual incident. That happened because the parents learned from their parents that all men are created equal and they are created with dignity by their creator. They learned that everyone deserves the respect of everyone else regardless of who they are. That is the kind of a heritage that Alex Patterson passed on to his children who then passed it on to their children. That is the lesson all of us need to learn from a man like Alex Patterson.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36 it is a privilege to present a petition which I am told is signed by approximately 47,000 Calgarians with respect to reforming the Young Offenders Act.
The petition begins with a reference to the late Ryan Garrioch, an honours student of 13 who I understand was killed by a 15-year old fellow student in his school yard. In closing, this is the largest petition by far that I have ever had the honour to present. I should note the anguish of Ryan's parents, Stu and Marg Garrioch, when they came to Ottawa recently with this petition. It is an honour as a fellow Albertan to accept their invitation to present it today.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Beatty that Bill C-62, an act respecting telecommunications, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Departmental envelope.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue the remarks I began before Question Period.
The central point I was dealing with was the fact that Bill C-62 was putting forward policy objectives. Those objectives designed a telecommunications system and policy which asserted clearly that the national govem-
Government Orders
ment's direction was going to be the overriding, ultimate authority for telecommunications policy in this country.
For the last seven or eight years this country has witnessed a government that year after year has worked against the principle it is enunciating today. Our national institutions, national programs and Crown corporations have served every region of our country, especially those regions that were very difficult to serve. We have had a total dismantling of many of those programs and institutions.
I have never hidden the fact that I am a strong centralist. I believe passionately in a strong national government. When I read the opening section of this bill, clause 7,1 could not believe it. It read like Liberal policy. This is a government that has been advocating constitutional arrangements time after time. Just recently the referendum was on a document that promoted a massive decentralized system. When I read this bill and found it approached our Canadian telecommunications policy in a comprehensive way where the national government had clear-cut authority, I was very pleased.
I must say that I believe this is what Canadians want. When we get to committee if every aspect of this bill meets the test of supporting the over-all broad policy objectives then I think this bill will have little difficulty in getting through this House.
Another point I want to make about the bill and about which some people are concerned is that there is definite direction in this bill for the cabinet or the Governor in Council to intervene from time to time to give direction to the CRTC. I personally have no problem with that.
One of the problems this country has is that there are too many instances where the bureaucracy has more control or gives more direction to the agenda than the elected politicians. Ultimately we are the ones responsible for the laws of this land. We are the ones responsible for the decisions that are taken in every region of this country and at every level of a particular department. Therefore, if from time to time the Governor in Council has to intervene and give direction on a certain aspect of our Canadian telecommunications policy I have abso-

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
lutely no difficulty with this. It will be held accountable in this House of Commons or in committee if a decision is faulty. Ultimately it will be held accountable with the electorate.
I suppose the natural concern when dealing with an agency like the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission is that we would be concerned about patronage opportunities. That type of accountability is the easiest to define and watch and thus cause the government to be answerable for its actions.
The other aspect of this bill that I thought I would touch on was clause 46. This is a very controversial clause and it is a very hot issue in my community and in urban areas right across the country. It has to deal with unsolicited telecommunications. "The commission" means the CRTC. Clause 46 reads:
The Commission may, by order, prohibit or regulate the carriage of any class of unsolicited telecommunications on the telecommunications facilities of a Canadian carrier to the extent that the Commission considers it necessary to prevent undue inconvenience or nuisance, giving due regard to freedom of expression.
I have had personal experience with this particular aspect of the law referring to the automatic or assisted dialling systems that certain companies use in our community. They use them in terms of the telephone and they also use them in terms of the fax machines.
Mr. Speaker, I have to tell you and through you the House that I have used such a system myself. About a year ago I heard about this system. It was a new technology. I could have my voice on tape and could give it to someone who had most of the phone numbers in the community on a computer. The computer would be programmed in such a way that my message could be delivered repeatedly.
About a year ago I used this system to promote the single-tax debate. I believe that tax reform is a fundamental issue in this country that needs review. I could not touch everyone in my community directly and certainly not everyone in my city of 2.5 million people so I hired one of these automatic dialling companies and within a month I talked to over 500,000 people. I did not personally talk to them. The person would be sitting at home and the telephone would ring. They would pick it up and there would be a taped voice. I started off the
conversation by saying: "Hello, I am Dennis Mills, the member of Parliament for Broadview-Greenwood. I would like to take a few seconds of your time to talk about tax reform. If you do not have the time all you have to do is hang up the phone".
Something that most people do not realize is that one is not forced to listen to the message. One is obviously forced to answer the phone if one is home, but if one is not interested in tax reform one just hangs up the phone and the message ceases.
I was able to communicate in about a 30-day period to about half a million people. I must say that I did get probably 10 to 15 complaints a day and people did say it was not a very polite way to communicate. However, I must say that I received at least 40, 50 or 60 phone calls a day from people who wanted more information and who wanted to get involved in the debate on tax reform.
I used it for only a month because I did feel there were aspects of it that were in poor taste but the idea of getting a very simple message to a number of people in a very short time is a very innovative technology.
I know there are police forces that use this automatic dialling service to give out emergency numbers and to warn people about crisis situations in their community. They will have all the numbers of a particular community on their computer and they will push the button and all of a sudden the police will communicate an emergency message to everyone in the community. That is a good use of the technology.
There are other times when it is in the public interest to use that technology. I think when we are examining this part of the bill that we are going to have to bring in some of the controversial people that have been cited for using this service. I think specifically in my city of the gentleman by the name of Marvin Fine who I am sure has caused a lot of fuss. I think he was the originator of this service and he has been using it for a lot of experimentation. I have told him directly that not all of his work is something that I agree with but he has used it for community work in a very effective way as well.
When we are analyzing this particular section of the act we have to be very careful how we define it and how we give regulation to it.
April 19, 1993

Government Orders
The same thing happens with fax machines. I have used the fax system myself to send out messages. Some days one gets people who thank you for the message. They like it. Then the next day one gets someone who will call in and say: "I want a cheque for 7 cents for the fact that you used my fax paper without seeking my permission". I know that clause 46 of this bill is a hotly contested part of the legislation.
The point is that the public at large has asked us to take a look at every aspect of the telecommunications policy in this country. The minister responsible for culture and communications has in fact taken up that challenge in this bill. Quite frankly, I think he has done a pretty good job.
My colleague from Mount Royal, our lead critic in this area, has said that in committee we will be rigorous in making sure that the policy objectives as stated in the preamble are followed through in the interpretive sections. We are totally supportive of those aspects of the bill where we encourage Canadian ownership. We are totally supportive of the aspects of the bill that encourage more research and development. We are totally supportive of the aspects of the bill that use the telecommunications industry to promote our sovereignty and give a sense of binding the regions and making sure that the rural regions have the same access for the same price as the major urban areas.
Over all, I am in support of this bill. I hope that the minister will be receptive to the amendments that once integrated into this bill will make it a piece of legislation that all of us in this House can be proud of. Ultimately it will be something that will enhance and support a sector of our economy, the telecommunications industry, which makes us the envy of the world.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on behalf of the New Democratic Party on this bill.
The member for Okanagan-Shuswap is our party's critic on this bill and will be speaking in the debate. I am the former critic of some time ago so I would like to speak on this. Some of the things I said when I was party critic now seem to me to be coming true.
The last member who spoke said that we in Canada are known for being one of the great countries in the world for telecommunications.
I could not agree more. Telecommunications and transportation is how we have created modem Canada. That is how we have created a modem, democratic and somewhat equitable Canada.
We are in the process of losing not only our lead in telecommunications but the old notion that we could have the best telephone service in the world for the average person. We had a regulated system that worked and now the government is changing this for ideological reasons. It is changing something that worked.
This bill reflects the Conservative government's insistence to deregulate and to privatize wherever conceivable. It is pure ideology and it is not the way to good government in my view.
While my colleagues and I have called for an updated telecommunications act to drive Canada into the 21st century, this is not the right vehicle. Make no mistake about it, this is a hugely important industry.
Canada's telecommunications industry generated $21 billion in revenue last year. It employs 125,000 people and it accounts for 8.6 per cent of our gross domestic product after inflation. It is currently governed by an antiquated act called the Railways Act. We govern our telecommunications by an act better attuned to railroads than to electronic superhighways, which we now have in Canada.
I will try to give an example of what I mean by the problem of deregulation, ideology and so on. I asked a question last year in the House of the present Minister of Communications. I was asking a question about Bell Telephone and about how the government had now allowed competition by Unitel and other companies with the telephone companies and the result of what that would mean to the phone service in Canada.
The Minister of Communications got up and said to quite a smiling House: "There is the NDP member defending the phone company. Wow, I have never seen anything like this". Everybody laughed, it was a great joke and so on. I thought at the time how little we have really thought through this matter.
The phone company, specifically Bell Telephone, is the largest company in Canada. Its real competition in North America is with American telecommunications where it is about eighth or ninth largest. That is where the real competition is.

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
Smart countries like Germany or Japan in their economic policies would start helping their major company. That would mean protecting their major company and not hurting it. The major company of Bell Telephone could in fact compete where it really competes. It could compete with strength in the North American market.
What does this government do? It deregulates in the local Canadian market. It allows competition in long distance calls. It forces the phone companies to compete and to lose money in putting up lower long distance rates and to become in many ways less competitive in the international scene where it really counts for Canada.
I ask the government to think a little bit ahead to the real competition. I find it ironic that it should have to come from an NDP member to tell the government what real competition means in the world. That is what it means.
We do not think this bill should be passed at second reading for a number of reasons. The first reason is simple. According to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms that you are an expert on, Mr. Speaker: "The second reading is the most important stage through which the bill is required to pass for its whole principle is then at issue and is affirmed or denied by a vote of the House".
Therefore this is a vote on the principle of this bill. However, according to the staff of the Minister of Communications, this bill will undergo substantial amendments during the committee stage. At one time the Department of Communications was asked to redraft the bill to take into account the substantial amendments recommended by the Senate Committee on Transport which engaged in a pre-study of this bill. It is clearly not correct for the House to pass a bill in principle which will be altered fundamentally at committee.
Government members may argue that the principle of the bill remains unchanged but this bill contains seven sweeping policy objectives. Changing any of these policy objectives in committee would undeniably alter the principle of the bill. Indeed we might not even be able to change them in committee, it would be out of order. The Senate committee recommended changes to these policy objectives. How can any members in this House pass legislation in principle when the true form of the
legislation will not be clear until the amendments are made?
We have precedents for this. The gun bill, of which I was a member of the committee, had quite a bit of disagreement concerning the original draft. The minister sent it to the justice committee of the House of Commons, not the Senate, the real committee where the real people are, for study and when we reported back another bill was drafted. The procedure actually worked.
This is what the government should do here. It should not ask the House to send the bill to committee while at the same time telling the House it is going to make major changes in the committee. It is not the right parliamentary procedure and a proper opposition should not vote for a bill like that.
A second and more substantial reason why it should not be passed is clear to anybody who pays a phone bill in Canada. That is a lot of people. I am talking about what has happened to people's phone bills. Have you looked at yours recently, Mr. Speaker? Phone bills are going up, just like cable rates are going up. But wages are not going up. Cable rates and phone bills are sure going up and they are going up pretty fast and pretty substantially.
They are going up for a number of reasons. In June 1992 the CRTC, the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission which supposedly regulates phone and cable companies decided to open up the long distance market. It accepted Unitel's application and assertion that long distance will not cost consumers more.
Let me pause a little bit and discuss Unitel. Unitel is Mr. Rogers and the cable people. Mr. Rogers, when he is the cable industry, has a monopoly and he milks it for all it is worth in increases in cable fees. He takes the money from the protected monopoly and he cream skims that monopoly, the cable industry, then he goes to the CRTC and he cries like a baby saying:"Boy, these phone companies have a monopoly here. I should be allowed to compete". He called it a communist, Leninist, Stalinist system. He said that we have to have competition. Of course he had the communist, Stalinist, Leninist system in the cable industry with the lack of competition but that is okay. He cream skims that, puts the money into Unitel and then starts competing with the phone companies.
April 19, 1993

What is the problem with that? Whatever Mr. Rogers and his friends want to do is fine except when it starts hurting the average Canadian consumer. Not only do they put it to the average Canadian on cable rates, then they take all that money, go into the phone industry and compete in long distance rates. The result is as I predicted until I was blue in the face in this House, in committee, before the CRTC that it would force local rates up and here is why. We have a system in which long distance rates subsidize local rates. We have higher long distance rates and lower local rates.
There have been two recent studies. One study was in Europe by the European Consumers Association. Another study was by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, the OECD, showing that Canada had lower rates.
We had a subsidy system and what happened? Who were the winners and losers? The people who made long distance calls had to pay a bit more, not a lot more because we are competitive according to the OECD but they had to pay a little more. Who are these people? You and I and the people who make the occasional long distance call, but by and large it is the big corporations who make the most long distance calls.
Who makes the local calls? It is the ordinary person. It is the local people and small business that make most of the local calls. Since we have had deregulation through the CRTC and through the ideological position of the government, we are now getting pressure to have higher local rates and lower long distance rates.
The phone companies say they cannot have lower long distance rates and still keep the same rates for our local calls. They have to survive somehow so they put up the local calls. Long distance calls come down, local calls go up. The winners are big companies; the losers are small businesses and individuals.
We told the CRTC until we were blue in the face and it still went ahead and did it. I challenge members of this House, both Liberals and Conservatives, to rebut this. Show me where competition has made the prices go down for the average person.
Bell Canada has applied to the CRTC for a rate increase. If its application is accepted, local rates will
Government Orders
jump as much as 65 per cent. BC TEL in my neck of the woods in British Columbia has asked for substantial rate increases as well, not only in their local rates but in directory assistance charges and service calls. Alberta Government Telephone also applied for a 30 per cent increase in local rates. I could go right across the provinces-up local rates, down long distance rates.
I want to say something to the unions that were involved in this. I worked in the past with the TWU, the Telecommunications Workers Union from British Columbia with my friend Rodney Hiebert and the people at that union. I addressed them directly on this. I also addressed the CEP, formerly the Communications Workers Union of Canada, which is the Bell union based in eastern Canada. We worked together. We told these unions and they told us that this would happen, that local rates would go up, long distance rates would go down and the average consumer would lose out.
They tell me that there is a B.C. corporation-is it B.C. Rail-involved with Unitel. They wonder what an agent of the British Columbia government, which after all is a progressive government, is doing with Unitel. I wondered too, quite frankly. What is it doing with Unitel? It is going to force up local rates for ordinary people. There is no way out. If long distance rates are lowered local rates have to be raised or the phone companies will go out of business. It is hurting the average individual. We should not have allowed the competition in long distance rates. People say it is inevitable and it had to be done. Nothing is inevitable.
We have a system in Canada where 98 per cent of people use the phone. We have a system where we have equality, where people in the north have more or less the same prices as people in the other areas. We will have a future system where the beneficiaries will be some big businesses in the major cities. The people in the rural areas and in the north will be paying more money. I predict that is what is going to happen. It is going to be the same with long distance rates.
When are the Canadian people going to wake up? They have seen what deregulation of the airlines did. The post office was practically deregulated and we have seen what that has done. Now we have seen what deregulation of the telephone industry has done and that is going to mean higher prices for the average Joe. That is what it means.

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
I also see that according to the government's own report-I love the way this is put: "The annual rate due to such changes"-that is the rates going up-"could amount to a drop-off rate of 2,500 to 7,500 subscribers across Canada". A drop-off rate of course is a nice way of saying that your aunt cannot afford her phone any more. Ninety-two per cent of Canadians were satisfied with their service.
I do not know but maybe I am too much of a conservative. I guess that is my problem. I believe if something is working, if it is not broken, why fix it? Why fix it so Mr. Rogers and his big business associates who contribute to the Conservative Party in a big way get their share? That is what it is. Who suffers but the average Canadian consumer?
We are not going to let this bill go so easily to committee. People want to know. People come to me in Coquitlam, Port Coquitlam and Port Moody in my riding, to my friend from northern Ontario and my friend from Nanaimo and say: "Look at these bills. My cable rates are going up". I showed them how they could say no, that they did not have to take the cable rates, but Rogers was not going to tell them that. Their cable rates are going up.
Now they are coming to me and saying: "My phone rates are going up but my pay cheque is not going up, and I am paying more in taxes. What is going on?" I will tell you what is going on. It is a pay-off to the friends of the Conservatives in this place. They say it is globalization and so on.
There is another reason why this bill should not be allowed second reading and it has to do with the North American free trade agreement, NAFTA, the agreement that the government is about to enter into without any real support from the Canadian people. It is a very smart government, is it not? Basically the free trade agreement fails because we lose employment, so what does the government do? We will sign another one with Mexico. Now that takes real brains, but the government proposes to do it.
The North American free trade agreement will grant foreign companies access to or the use of Canadian telecommunications networks and services "on reasonable and non-discriminatory terms and conditions". That is the phrase, reasonable and non-discriminatoiy terms and conditions. When I see a phrase like that I worry. In other words, on terms and conditions no less favourable than those accorded to Canadian companies.
The chapter goes much further. It limits the terms and conditions that Canada will be able to impose in the future. Here is the kicker. Specifically legislators will be required to ensure that prices charged for telephone services are based on the economic costs directly related to providing such services. Although NAFTA would allow cross-subsidization between our existing telephone companies to continue, we will not be able to require resellers to make the contribution payments that are necessary to support universal service.
This bill does nothing to prevent the erosion of cross-subsidization. The bill actually encourages deregulation regardless of its effects on consumers and small businesses. In fact it takes us even further. We get into the free trade agreement which will make it impossible for any future government, any progressive government that may happen to be elected to make changes, any government that wants to come to the defence of the Canadian consumer.
We need a system where we pay attention to the universality in services. This is a big country and it is a northern country. That means we have to serve the people in northern and rural areas. They have to have communications. We have to keep the cost as low as possible.
We have to take our big companies like BC Tel and Bell and help them compete in the international scene where it really matters for Canada. That is the basis for a communications policy that is different than the policy of the government. That is why we in the New Democratic Party differ with the government on this bill.
I could go on and give other reasons why the bill should not go to committee but I have finished. I will close by making a plea on behalf of the poor consumers of Canada who are getting it put to them on cable rates and phone rates. I ask the government to please listen to their voices. Cut this ideology of deregulation and stop harming a very good phone system by this nonsense of
April 19, 1993

helping your friends in Unitel and the other places and putting it to the Canadian consumer.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of interest to my colleague from Port Moody-Coquitlam. He now has the pleasure of being the critic in matters of justice but he was the critic in telecommunications and culture prior to that. I know he has some very strong feelings about the role and place of cable and what we should be doing with respect to cable and the question of convergence with regard to cable and telephony. I am curious to know if he is satisfied with the covering of the concerns of the cable and telephone industries. Why does he consider this bill to be a total deregulation? I believe the most important aspect of this bill is to provide a universal, affordable and accessible telephone system for Canadians at the local level. Protection of that service is inherent and must be pursued. While we are interested in telecommunications as the most forward-moving technology for the pursuit of improved jobs and job creation, it is not at the cost in any way, shape or form of a universal, accessible and affordable telephone system for all Canadians.
If the hon. member thinks this is under threat and a total deregulation, I wonder if he would pursue that matter somewhat or clarify it at least.

Mr. Speaker, I must acknowledge the expertise of my colleague, the member for Mount Royal who is the Liberal critic in this area and has consistently followed this issue in the committee. I pay tribute to her for that. She is a very keen observer of this area.
May I just take a moment in responding to this? The hon. member has difficulty with my riding. I used to represent the riding of Vancouver-Kingsway. Due to redistribution and the movement to the suburbs I now represent a riding called Port Moody-Coquitlam, which is an eastern suburb about 30 kilometres from Vancouver. It is snuggled up against the west coast mountains and is a very beautiful, booming and dynamic community. Port Moody was the terminus of the transcontinental railway where the first train came until, of course, the real estate developers thought they could make more money in Vancouver and moved the terminus into Vancouver, according to Pierre Burton. That is the
Government Orders
riding, Port Moody-Coquitlam. Coquitlam means salmon in Indian. It is a very nice name. It is a very fast-growing area with lots of cable subscribers and lots of telephone users.
I too am committed, as I think the hon. member is committed, to an affordable system, universal and so on. In my speech I was pointing out the dangers. I pick up principles in this bill that extend and use the wording again of deregulation, of the kind of neo-conservative agenda of government. I think that is a real concern in communications. I think it will lead us in the wrong direction.
There is an area for competition in communications. There is also an area for working with our stronger companies and using regulation and sometimes restraint of trade to help them. I am thinking of Bell. I took a lot of flak by saying that in the House. I tried to explain it today on the basis of building up the strongest companies and then competing at the international level where the real competition is.
As I said, the hon. member is more of an expert than I am with regard to cable. I will listen carefully when she speaks further on this matter here and in committee. However, it seems to me that the wording of the bill and some of the phrases lead into this deregulation language. That again leads to the problems we had in communication, which can be specifically seen in how we have a system where cable is half regulated and other parts are not. There is an 8 per cent increase and then a 300 per cent increase in the area that is not regulated. The phone seems totally regulated, but there is a push to get more money for local services. It seems to me we are putting ourselves into that bind.
I think we have to look at the fundamental principles before we can vote on the principle of a telecommunications bill like this.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I can just make a comment and then ask the member a quick question. Clause 7 of Bill C-62 states:
It is hereby affirmed that telecommunications performs an essential role in the maintenance of Canada's identity and sovereignty and that the Canadian telecommunications policy has as its objectives

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
(a) to facilitate the orderly development in Canada of a telecommunications system that serves to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, social, political and economic fabric of Canada;
At the same time I look at the Wall Street Journal of Tuesday, February 9, 1993 and see the AT&T advertisement essentially saying that in 1993 the border between Canada and the U.S. will no longer be a barrier.
AT&T has purchased an operating interest in Unitel, the corporation directly responsible for the breakdown and deregulation within the telecommunications system. I wonder if the member would comment on whether he thinks this act protects Canada's identity and sovereignty. Will the culmination of the free trade agreement, the North America free trade agreement and this bill further erode the sovereignty in the areas of communications and transportation within Canada?

The problem is that we will not be able to require resellers of services to make the contribution payments necessary to support the universal service, in other words to cross-subsidize the local rate. The resellers will be people like AT&T.
AT&T, American Telephone and Telegraph, the largest company in the world could swallow the Canadian market in a hiccup. Its advertisement in the Wall Street Journal said: "In 1993 this border will no longer be a barrier". In other words, these companies will be allowed to come into Canada under this legislation as resellers. They will not have to cross-subsidize the lower markets. This will erode the first principle of the bill the member read and will lead to increased foreign control of our Canadian market just as we are doing in the airline industry.
Soon we will not have the Canadian border at all. It will be gone and these large companies will come in. If we want to have an independent country we have to fight for it. If we want to continue to have legislation and deals like this we are going to lose this country. That is what we are saying and why we are opposing this bill.
