speechtext:
Before resuming debate it is my duty pursuant to Standing Order 38 to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Hillsborough-Veterans Affairs; the hon.
member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Montreal Economy; the hon. member for Don Valley East-Cyprus; the hon. member for Bonavista-Trinity-Conception-National Defence; the hon. member for London East-Municipal Taxation.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in this debate on Bill C-62, an act respecting telecommunications. It addresses so many concerns and complaints I have been hearing at the constituency office, town hall meetings as recently as last week, and from just talking to businesses and individual residents within Parkdale-High Park.
The concerns that have been raised fall into about five categories which are CB radios, unscrupulous advertising between post office and Bell telephone, unscrupulous telemarketing techniques, the PC Cops computer automated dialing program, which I want to share with the House and junk mail.
I agree that this is a very important bill. The direct advertising industry employs 100,000 Canadians. There are a lot of jobs in the high tech area. It generates over $20 billion in revenues. It truly is the railway into the year 2000 and beyond. This bill will probably start laying the rails and the new super tracks for this direction.
Our critic for the Liberal Party stated the importance of this bill when she said: "Canada needs a harmonized set of rules and regulations to give all Canadians equal access to telecommunications and the information revolution". That sums up the importance of this bill.
Let us look at the process this bill has undergone. I recall when the former Minister of Finance addressed this issue in his 1984 budget. I am looking at the date by the table officers. It says April 19, 1993. Where have we been since 1984?
Other budgets have addressed this. Then the Minister of Communications introduced the bill on February 27, 1992. Today it is April 19, 1993. Where has the minister been for 14 months? For 14 months the bill has not been touched. I can lay it two to one that before the debate is over on this bill, the minister will probably bring in closure or time allocation limiting debate on this important and extensive bill.
April 19, 1993

Let me begin with the first set of concerns my constituents have been calling me about, which is the whole area of CB radios. When we were in government an owner of a CB radio had to buy a licence. It was registered so it was known who the owner of that radio was, the serial number of the CB radio, et cetera. Then the Conservative government came in and in its almost psychotic move to deregulate everything, deregulated the need for CB ownership and use. Now anyone can go into a store, a child of eight or nine or any person, purchase a CB radio and go on the air with no regulations and no holds barred.
I had a problem with two organizations competing for the same airwaves and running quite a feud over the airwaves so all the rest of the people could listen in. If it was just innocent listening I would not mind but there was a blockage of the airwaves. They would set screechy noises up to the radio microphone so no one could hear what the words were.
Then came the swearing and cursing. This was not language fit for the airwaves. I addressed this to the former Minister of Communications and the present minister. To date, nothing has been done. I must give some credit to the bureaucrats. They came to Parkdale and tried to bring some peace to the airwaves but they could not.
Then came the harassment of women. I thought I had heard everything, but I have never heard such foul language as I heard on the CB airwaves in my own riding. The foul language was harassing women. What some of these men on the radio waves did to debase women is not what I want in Canada. I see the minister shaking his head. That is not what he wants for Canada. We want standards in Canada for the telephone, the radio airwaves and in the press. This is why Canada was named the number one country by the United Nations last year. It is because we did have standards, whether those standards concerned TV, radio or telephone.
However, two ministers could not eliminate the kind of harassment some of the women in my riding of Parkdale-High Park are still putting up with. I am not pulling this out of the air. I asked people who were harassed to send me copies of the tapes. One person did.
Government Orders
I shared some of those copies with our critic and then sent them directly to the minister.
This has been going on since I was re-elected in 1988. We cannot clean up the CB airwaves. What kind of a government are we? If we cannot clean up this kind of harassment of women in our society, we are not fit to govern. I hope the minister, who although he is not sitting in this House I am sure is watching this debate on TV, will take it to heart. Hopefully this bill will also assist in helping us to clean up the airwaves for the CB radios.
The second group of complaints I have been getting and which this bill addresses concerns the unscrupulous uses of advertising. I am not talking about the strict telemarketing techniques. I am talking about what is going on between a Crown corporation, Canada Post, and Bell Canada.
The postal person delivers flyers to people's homes. I am sure it does not happen only in my riding where unemployment is so high. It is the first time in history that the unemployment rate in a large city like Toronto is higher than the national average. It is heart-breaking to see these people, who have used up their unemployment insurance and do not want to go on welfare, come begging for jobs. They get a flyer delivered to the door and what does it read? "Employment opportunities. Make up to $500 a week, guaranteed $15 an hour". Who would not jump at that? If I were unemployed and using up my UI and did not want to go on welfare would I not read this flyer? Would I not do what this flyer instructs me to do?
What happens with this flyer that is delivered to our homes by the post office? Someone who is unemployed will pick up the phone and call, all excited because there is a job waiting, but it is a scam. By making that call the person has to pay $10 minimum. The person is unemployed and has used up his or her UI. Some are on welfare and some do not want to go on welfare. However, we get these jokers pulling a scam like this on hundreds and thousands of Canadians. Is that what Canada is all about? Are those the standards we want in our country? Is that what we are all about?
The scam is that $10 is paid but there is no job in the end. There is a special 1-900 phone number to call and they are asked to send a resume. They send a resume but they do not hear from these people. A whole year goes

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
by and still there is no job. It is a scam. I do not know what else to call it.
The poorest of this country's poor are being taken because of this government's psychosis to deregulate everything. "Private enterprise can do it all. Government has no role. It should not interfere." It is time that someone does interfere to clean up the mess the Tories have got this country into over the last nine years. I would hate to think what would happen to Canada if they were in government for another nine years.
I apologize for speaking with such strength and almost anger. When one sees how these people have been taken it does make one cry.
Let us look at the telemarketing advertising techniques themselves, which are increasing. Most of the complaints I receive are about these. The hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood admitted that he had used this technique himself to promote his single tax system. At least he was polite enough to tell the listener very early in the message: "If this message is not for you, please hang up".
It still does not stop the phone from being in use. Last week I had appointments in my constituency office. The other lines were busy but I thought the main line was open. I picked it up and there was a telemarketing message. I had to wait 10 minutes before I could use my own telephone. Because my telephone is controlled by the computer, it tied my constituency line up for 10 minutes. I really have a question of privilege because my duties as a member of Parliament were being denied. My carrying out my role and calling my constituents was hampered by this technique.
There is no need for that. CRTC can set a time limit on these messages. They do not have to be 10 minutes. They could be one-minute messages or maybe two minutes maximum. If you cannot say what you want to say in one minute then do not say it. We make a lot of statements before Question Period in this House of Commons and they are one-minute statements. I think we say quite a bit in that one minute.
One complaint I received from a constituent was that she was trying to get a doctor but could not because her phone was tied up with a telemarketing message. Someone complained because they could not get a 911 number during an emergency. Let us say there is an emergency
and a child is suffocating or someone has a heart attack and minutes count. Seconds count. One cannot wait 10 minutes for that telemarketing message to finish before dialing 911 or phoning emergency.
Is that what we want in our country? Are those the standards we want? I say no. Then there are the complaints I get from the owners of cellular telephones. They are in the car and get a telemarketing message. They do not like it so they hang up but the message goes for 10 minutes. What do they pay for, one minute? No, they pay for 10 minutes. Is that fair?
I understand the bill is going to address some of these problems. If it does, I will support this bill. This bill can address a lot of the issues I am raising here. They are people issues. They are not fictitious issues. They are day-to-day people issues, issues affecting people daily.
That is why I am so pleased we have such a strong critic on our side. Any time I received one of these complaints and referred it to her she followed it up. I see a lot of those concerns brought in to the bill. Whatever the committee was doing or saying, I think someone has been listening.
Let me give an example of where this technology can be useful. I am not blocking modem technology or future technology, no. That is the route we have to go. I think that is where the jobs are for Canadians in the future. We should address this as a nation.
The problem with our education system is that it comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces, but who sets the direction for the country for the next 20 or 50 years? It should be the federal government laying out clear goals for the next 50 years. Then the provinces could build their curriculums based on these goals. Then we would have direction and would not be stuck with the 1.5 million jobless we have today.
I promised to give an example of how this technology can be used positively. The Metropolitan Toronto Police, No. 11 division is in my constituency and has introduced the PC Cops computer system. Groups such as the Neighbourhood Watch programs, the Sunnyside and the Swansea rate payer groups, High Park, Runnymede and Jane Street rate payers associations, Roncevalles, Bloor West Village, the Junction Business Association and the local Villager newspaper, all co-operated with the police on the PC Cops computer system.
April 19, 1993

This system asks people to register if they would like to be on this telemarketing system. It is a computer phone system. Everyone registered gets the messages. What kinds of messages are sent by computer? Messages if there is a missing child, if there is a break-in in the community, assaults. Everyone who is registered gets this call by computer. If there is any kind of criminal activity in the community, the whole community is notified and it does not take 10 minutes. The message is only one minute. If this bill were to do anything to limit telemarketing messages to one minute then it would be doing a great service. These messages go through in 60 seconds. The introduction by the Metropolitan Toronto Police of this PC Cops computer program is an excellent use of this modem technology.
I do want to raise the concerns of Robert Morie and Ed Radonic from my riding. They have small businesses and they say their businesses are being interrupted with junk mail. The fifth issue I said I get a lot of complaints about is the junk mail on the fax machine. It really affects a small business when the fax machine is tied up continually with junk mail. We get faxes in Ottawa but again it is appropriate use of the fax machine. In the morning I see piles of fax sheets all the way down to the floor but they are about the present crisis in the former Yugoslavia where people have relatives and friends. They fax me messages because they are concerned about their relatives. Again I am not knocking this modem high technology. I think it is good, but let us put it to positive use.
I am glad the minister came in to the House. I am sure he will take the concerns of my constituents in Park-dale-High Park and address them in the bill so we will have a good bill in the end.

Mr. Speaker, the minister has been in the House to hear what the hon. member has had to say. My colleague always brings some very interesting and serious concerns to the attention of this House. He is obviously one who listens very carefully to his constituents.
I was quite interested in what he had to say about what seems to be a serious abuse of this new technology. I think it could work in a very positive way in the interests of the consumer and the business world. I do not think they are necessarily mutually exclusive goals. I do think there should be informed consent and he put it best by
Government Orders
saying to put the names on a list, something of that nature.
I was intrigued while I was listening to the hon. member speak. I must say that some of the things he clarified in his presentation came as quite a surprise. I went back to see what the Privacy Commissioner had to say. He shares a lot of the hon. member's concerns, but he makes three fundamental points which are very important. I would hope the hon. member's constituents in terms of the concerns he has brought to my attention and to the attention of the people of Canada through his remarks today would find comfort in the observations of the Privacy Commissioner. Of course there has to be freedom of expression in this country. It is fundamental in the Canadian charter and is balanced by what is reasonable and justifiable in section 1.
The Privacy Commissioner said that the first ingredient would be that of informed consent. In other words, you know what you are asking for, you put your name on the list and therefore you agree that your name could be used. If you do not agree then they have no right to use it. The second was that it would not be costly. There would be a cost neutrality.
The hon. member talked about the fact that this was not cost neutral. It was an awful teasing. It was an unpleasant and unjust experience where people were looking for work and this fraud took place. There has to be some way in which it is cost neutral and we have a way of verifying what is the content in the message that is to go out. You cannot hide behind the fact that you do not know what the content is. I think that is the message the hon. member was giving. That would be found in the third agreement which the member says should be open and transparent.
I would like to ask my hon. colleague a question. If informed consent, cost neutrality and openness or transparency were in place, would the hon. member agree that this new technology could be in the interest not only of the telemarketer but the constituents who would want to use this new technology?

Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what we need. There will be many bills related to and affected by this bill. If all that is put into place as recommended by the Privacy Commissioner, it would go a long way in satisfying the concerns of my constituents.

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
I mentioned the PC Cops program. Everyone knows they are registered. The police asked for contributions but they also stressed very clearly that they do not have to make a contribution to participate in the program. A financial contribution would be appreciated but it is not required for participation.
Many of my constituents have difficulty with English as new Canadians. They will call and unknowingly they are charged the $10. The $10 is in fine print down at the bottom. They phone looking for a job and then they get a $10 bill because it is hidden in small print. My constituents would certainly be very pleased if as our critic said these issues could be guaranteed.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be given the opportunity to address this particular piece of legislation. Most Canadians who have been listening to my colleagues will by now have no doubt noted that this is a major piece of legislation. We are talking about an electronic railroad, something of which Canadians can be very proud in the future.
We are talking about a major industry. Over 100,000 individuals are affected in terms of jobs by the communications industry and there are over $20 billion of expenditures. It is really what one could consider a strategic industry for the future, for Canada, for Canadians. It will have good jobs, I hope long-term, well remunerated positions for young people and those who want to change employment.
I say that because I think it is particularly important we take the time to discuss this thoroughly. As I indicated it is a major piece of legislation.

This bill is very important in several ways. It is not only about the future but about good, well-paid, long-term jobs.
This is something that should be considered very seriously and carefully.

Some people are going to be asking why though. If my information is correct this was introduced over a year ago. It appears to have been stalled in terms of going to the legislative committee for some time. Why is there a
big rush at this particular point in time? I mean people will be asking the inevitable question: Was government not thinking this through? Did it not plan appropriately? I suppose some will say that there does not appear to be any particular raison d'etre, planification, rationalisation. Why the rush at this particular point in time?
There are some positive features in this bill that my colleagues have spoken about in an attempt to come to grips with a major industry in Canada, something that is growing and something that is here today and has been with us for some time but opens tremendous opportunities for the future.
Some concerns have been voiced. For example, I have received calls and correspondence from individuals who have wondered and have asked whether or not the local rates would in fact be affected as a result of the legislation. Will they increase and, if so, by how much? I have received some calls from seniors. These individuals sometimes want to use the telephone rather extensively because of limited mobility and what have you. I also received some from poor families, people who already have a great deal of difficulty meeting their objective to meet the daily needs of their families with their meagre resources.
Of course among those poor are single parent families most often headed by mothers. If local rates are going to be affected, if they are going to increase, if there are going to be substantial increases, we really need to be particularly concerned. I have assured them that I believe this is not necessarily the case. I hope what I have said is in fact correct. I certainly would like to have some confirmation of it.
Some other individuals have asked whether or not this is in fact a bargaining chip being used by the government in terms of its North American free trade agreement. Just to make sure that I reflect their views correctly, I want to quote what was said to me. They believe that this bill would lead to the selling off of our telecommunications industry and of course the loss of Canadian jobs, particularly today when we are in a recession and there are many people unemployed, well over 1.6 million people. There are great difficulties being experienced by Canadians who want to work. This is of great concern to those particular individuals, not only those who are unemployed but those who still have jobs and really want to be able to maintain them.
April 19, 1993

There again I would hope that this is not-and I believe it is not; if I am wrong I hope someone will correct me-an attempt to take the first step toward making sure that Americans can buy into this particular industry which I consider very Canadian. We happen to be in the forefront. We happen to be world leaders and I want us to stay there. I want to make sure that whatever progress is made can be made in co-operation with other countries, that we retain the leadership and that we continue to make the discoveries that are going to benefit Canada and Canadians generally.

As I just said, there is opposition from some people, and I mentioned two areas. Some people believe that residential telephone rates might go up. Of course there are those who wonder if this would lead to the selling off of our telecommunications industry or if the government as a result of a risky involvement with the United States might lose control of an industry which is perceived as "belonging" to Canada.

One thing these people have asked is: "What are you people going to be doing with this bill? Will you be supporting it?" Yes, we will, providing certain conditions are met. I just want to share with my colleagues and people who may be listening some of the concerns and some of the things we want.
Liberals continue to believe in a strong Canadian telecommunications system that provides universal, affordable, reliable and modem basic telephone service for Canadians from coast to coast. This is particularly important in a large country such as ours where often there are small communities isolated from larger centres and where there is a need to communicate.
As a result of our desire for this type of system, my colleagues in the Liberal Party and I agree that complete deregulation of this sector is not really in the public interest.
We also agree that Canada must have a regulatory system that meets Canadian goals. I think that is very important. It must meet Canadian goals and should not be weakened through either the North American free trade talks or the GATT talks. I think that is of exceptional importance. We can still be involved with NAFTA if that is to be the case and with GATT, but we
Government Orders
need to make sure that whatever happens we protect our own particular interests.
My colleagues and I also believe that this bill should provide a fresh direction for the telecommunications sector so it can maximize the benefits to every Canadian of the world-wide information revolution in terms of learning, literacy, education, training and communicating.
Let me just very quickly dwell on a few of the problems that have been brought to my attention. Some people would suggest that there needs to be some major changes. There are problems with the definitions clause, clause 2, for example how hybrid companies will be dealt with. On the power of direction, the government did establish power of direction. However it has also maintained the power to vary or rescind CRTC decisions at the same time which mitigates against that.
There are also concerns with respect to exemptions. For example, some of my colleagues and I are not convinced that exemptions for certain classes of carriers should be in the bill itself. As well the vary or rescind power by Governor in Council should be replaced we believe by the set aside or refer back power now in use. We believe this latter alternative is superior.
As well there are concerns about provincial consultation, tactical standards, ministerial authority to grant licences to carriers, and those are but some of the examples. I should point out that there are also no provisions in this bill for Canadian ownership and control of our telecommunications system. Although I understand there may be an ideological difference between the government and this party over that, there ought to be provisions for Canadian ownership and control of our telecommunications system.
I want to make the following point which I consider equally important. As this legislation proceeds I shall and so will my colleagues be working with colleagues from all parties for changes in the bill to ensure we maintain a telecommunications system which is Canadian owned, which enhances the international competitiveness of Canadian industry and which serves as a unifying communications link among all Canadians at this difficult time in our history. As I indicated before, I want to stress that while there are a number of positive features in this bill there are a number of opportunities to improve it. I do not pretend I have identified all the major concerns, but certainly if one looks at my remarks and the remarks of my colleagues that have been made in this House I think we can have a better final product.

April 19, 1993
Government Orders

As I just said, the government has taken some positive steps in certain sectors, but there are still some flaws that should be corrected. I would really like the minister and his government to listen not only to what I am saying but to what all of us have said in order to try if possible to correct, the situation, to be more responsive to Canadians' needs to ensure that it remains our system, that we can improve it, that we will keep the best jobs for Canadians and that we can remain leaders in this critical sector for Canada's future.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to Bill C-621 should point out that part of the problem those of us in my party are having with this bill is that the minister in his remarks this morning made it very clear that the bill is going to need substantial changes. Yet it is difficult for us to be able to determine whether at second reading stage this bill should be allowed to go forward as is with the idea that there will be other perhaps substantial and substantive changes in the direction of the bill without knowing ahead of time exactly what those are.
I have a question for the Elouse and for the minister. If there are substantial and perhaps substantive changes to be made to this bill it might make more sense to simply withdraw Bill C-62 or leave it where it is until the time comes when the bill can in fact be set out to the House in the terms and direction in which the government wishes to take the bill.
It would certainly be handy from our point of view, if there have been substantial changes already drafted, to be able to look at some of those changes with respect to the bill before us. I say to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, that I think it would be of assistance to those of us on this side of the House to know the direction in which it is going. Perhaps if there are going to be
substantial changes the minister might want to consider at this stage withdrawing the bill and putting forth the bill as it will ultimately be put forward.
In speaking directly on the bill I would like to refer to clause 7 of the bill. For the purposes of those watching the debate and for the purposes of those who will perhaps want to look at Hansard as bedtime reading in the future I would like to read clause 7 and make comments on it. It is the Canadian telecommunications policy and objectives.
It is hereby affirmed that telecommunications performs an essential role in the maintenance of Canada's identity and sovereignty in that the Canadian telecommunications policy has as its objectives
(a)	to facilitate the orderly development in Canada of a telecommunications system that serves to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, social, political and economic fabric of Canada;
(b)	to render reliable and affordable telecommunications services of high quality accessible in both urban and rural areas in all regions of Canada;
(c)	to enhance the efficiency and competitiveness, at the national and international levels, of Canadian telecommunications;
(d)	to promote the ownership and control of Canadian carriers by Canadians;
(e)	to promote the use of Canadian transmission facilities for telecommunications within Canada and between Canada and points outside Canada;
(f)	to foster increased reliance on market forces for the provision of telecommunications services;
(g)	to stimulate research and development in Canada in the field of telecommunications and to encourage innovation in the provision of telecommunications services; and
(h)	to respond to the economic and social requirements of users of telecommunications services, including the protection of the privacy of individuals.
With the advance of technology, particularly transportation and communications technology, it is essential that we have an updated and upgraded telecommunications bill. We must have a bill that looks at what is in the present, learning from mistakes of the past, but with a view to the projections of what will or might occur in the future.
April 19, 1993

Certainly from the perspective of one who is not well versed in telecommunications matters, but like everybody else in Canada is well aware of how telecommunications has weaselled its way into our everyday living, the Canadian telecommunications policy appears to be a policy set out that can well do the job if in fact we set out our policies and our legislation as laid out in those eight particular subsections that I have read into the record.
Let us just analyse what has happened in Canada and what is happening at present. We can perhaps have a projection of what probably, as a result of the past and the present, will happen in the future.
Look at the policies of this government and the policies as set out in Bill C-62 coupled with the policies that it set out in the past through the free trade agreement and the North American free trade agreement. Are these going to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, social, political and economic fabric of Canada?
If we look at the direction that has been taken I question whether the sovereignty of our communications systems is being protected. Look at the over-all pattern of deregulation that has been a trademark of this government for the past eight and a half years in the transportation system and the privatization of such things as Canada Post. Have we protected our sovereignty within these areas? Have we enriched our social, cultural and political fabric?
I would suggest that we have not. If we look at the bill and at what is happening within the North American free trade agreement, then it appears that NAFTA would grant foreign companies access to or use of the Canadian telecommunications network and services on "reasonable and non-discriminatory terms and conditions". In other words, this would be on terms and conditions no less favourable than those accorded to the Canadian companies.
Government Orders
that developed and cross-subsidized local rates within the telephone network.
Here is what happened with Unitel. AT&T, the giant telecommunications network, has purchased a 20 per cent interest in Unitel and is using it as a method of getting into the Canadian telecommunications network.
This is of some concern to me. The bill itself protects Canadian companies in the situation where it will only allow 20 per cent of the telephone company to be owned by a non-Canadian or foreign company. That is positive. However, if we look at the advertisement of AT&T, it appears to show us that it considers this as a method of breaking down the border between the two countries. In fact, it is their first foot in the door. Their excess capacity in a corporation of that size is so substantial that it could swallow up the whole system within Canada without blinking an eye or without having to swallow particularly hard.
Let us look at clause 7 where it says:
to render reliable and affordable telecommunications services of
high quality accessible in both urban and rural areas
This brings up the problem of what has been called, within the area, cross-subsidization. It is the provision that allowed companies to use increased long distance rates in order to subsidize and ensure that regional disparities, where it cost more to take telephone lines into a rural area, are made reasonable so that everybody within that area has telephone service available to them. This included companies such as BC Tel in my home province, Alberta Government Telephone in Alberta, Bell Telephone in Ontario and in some of the other provinces as well as Sask Tel in Saskatchewan.
However, it also deals with local rates for basic telephone service. My colleague from Kamloops pointed out what was occurring in his area with respect to telephone rates. He pointed out in his speech a number of cities within the United States where there has been deregulation and what the local rates are there.
I look with some concern over the bid and I have If one recalls, the rates varied from something like $26 spoken on this before. I have presented petitions on up to $47 in various parts of the United States for local behalf of hundreds of constituents within my riding on telephone rates. However, in most areas in British the successful bid of Unitel to enter into the long Columbia the local telephone rates are anywhere in the distance market essentially on the backs of companies area from $11 to $14 or $15.

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
It is interesting that this debate should come up at this time because on April 12 I received a letter dated April 1, 1993 from the BC Tel Company signed by E.L. Patterson, the executive vice-president and chief operating officer. In the first paragraph he said: "Today BC Tel announced its intention to file an application with the CRTC early this summer for a general rate increase. We also applied today for interim local rate increases. The proposed interim rate increases range from $4.05 to $4.15 for residential customers and $3.05 to $4.15 for business customers".
During the debates and in the petitions that I presented to the House and that others in my party presented to the House, we constantly reminded the government of some of the experiences in the United States with deregulation within the communications networks down there and the probability that there would be a loss of jobs as well as increased local rates for telephone users.
If I go on with this letter from Mr. Patterson, I would quote two paragraphs within the body of that letter. He points out: "Historically telecommunications in Canada has been regulated by social rather than economic policy considerations. Local rates have been subsidized by long distance revenues in order to provide universal access to the telephone. In fact BC Tel cross-subsidizes local service with 60 cents of every dollar of long distance revenue. To achieve this subsidy the price of long distance service has been kept artificially high.
With the introduction of long distance competition this historical balance has been changed. Competition brings many benefits to customers. However, as competitors claim an increased market share, the subsidy available for basic service diminishes. While some competitors are required to contribute to local service, their contribution is significantly less than BC Tel. As well, few people realize that BC Tel is currently required to subsidize our competitors' entry into the market; competitors which now include AT&T, the world's largest telecommunications company".
If I go on and look at that one side it is obvious that the rates of local service are going up, as we predicted. If we look at one of the government's studies we can also see that there will be rate increases not only to consumers but to small businesses as well.
A briefing document from the Department of Communications discusses the effects of long distance competition. It says that the competition will require gradual decreases and cross-subsidization and therefore increased rates. This will hit residential and small business users hardest while big business users will benefit.
In the same briefing document the Department of Communications quotes a Peat Marwick study which suggested that local rate increases over five years of between 13 per cent and 93 per cent would be required. This would represent 2 per cent to 12 per cent per annum. It is interesting to note that this government document also mentions a drop-off rate and states that the annual drop-off rate due to such changes could amount to 2,500 to 7,500 subscribers across Canada.
What is a drop-off rate? It is simply a nice way to tell Canadians that this is the number of people who are no longer able to afford to have a telephone in their own home.
It seems that the affordability that is looked for in this legislation is slowly slipping away from not only the regular consumer but from the small business person who will have added costs as a result of this.
From the point of view of employment it is interesting that on April 16 Brian Canfield, the president of BC Tel, announced that the company is working to reduce its staff size by 4 per cent this year. It has already seen 422 employees accept volunteer separation packages.
In a news release Mr. Canfield said: "The entry into the Canadian market of the U.S. phone giant AT&T, which bought 20 per cent of Unitel after the CRTC last year approved Unitel's entry into the long distance field, added weight to BC Tel's argument that inflated long distance rates should not be used to subsidize artificially low local rates. It is ludicrous that BC Tel should be put
April 19, 1993

in a position where we must indirectly subsidize AT&T, the world's largest telecommunications company".
It appears that what is happening with the direction of telecommunications legislation and the telecommunications network in Canada is that it is becoming less affordable for Canadians and we are losing jobs as a result of the policies that have been set out. I hope the direction the government chooses shores up some of what has already been lost in ensuring that Canadians are granted sovereignty over their telecommunications systems and that Canadians are assured of affordable telephone and telecommunications systems within Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with some interest to the member's speech. One of the areas of concern that he has flagged is the situation as it relates to how employees of the different companies that are involved in telecommunications will be treated under the new legislation.
I am very interested in knowing from the member and his party how they feel this particular piece of legislation will adversely affect the working men and women who are involved in the telecommunications field.
In looking at the bill it seems to me that what we are doing is standardizing regulations in a broader sense. Instead of having all these different provinces being able to do their own thing they will have more consultation with the federal government and have a system that goes across the board. It is hoped that in the long term, it may not be so obvious in the short term, this will put in work rules for individuals across the board and give them the opportunity to be heard, and of course at the same time give them the kind of work rules we would like for our workers in Canada.
Being one of those people who advocates national standards and national rules, and I had assumed that the member who just spoke and his party felt the same way, I would be interested in knowing why the hon. member's party seems to think that this would be a step backward for workers in this particular industry instead of a step forward, as I think it is.

Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to look at the bill itself. I think the remarks I made at the start of
Government Orders
my speech made it very clear that the direction in which the government wants to go is so foggy that we cannot actually see where we are ultimately going to be as a result of the legislation.
I made suggestions that perhaps, as was done with the UI bill, this bill should simply be allowed to die. The direction the government wants to go should be put into a bill to give us some direction as to where it intends to take us in this legislation.
I agree with the member who posed the question that changes must be made in the legislation. There is no doubt about that. We are now in a situation where things have changed so substantially just within our lifetime that it is not good enough to try to depend on old legislation that is out of sync with what is happening nowadays.
If we look specifically at the regulation of the industry we can see that this legislation appears to be dumping off some of the responsibilities we have given to the CRTC in the past back into the political field. Every decision the CRTC will make from now on will be diminished with respect to regulation.
I am somewhat sceptical about whether it will help or hinder the proper regulation across Canada if we have constant interference of the politicians within the system as opposed to regulation by the CRTC.

Mr. Speaker, in his remarks the hon. member for Okanagan-Similka-meen-Merritt spent some time discussing the problems that some of the provincial telephone companies are having with government legislation relating to the forced integration of those companies' infrastructures into national services provided by competition from outside and inside the country.
We have a government that is very taken with maintaining the right to intellectual property under the GATT and has provided legislative changes in this Chamber up to and including extensions to copyright and patent legislation and eliminating our licence system for patented drugs. Can the member enlighten us as to why the government is pursuing that range of proposals securing the right to property and to systems that are in existence yet is attempting to create competition through the imposition of AT&T and Intertel, et cetera, on the provincial telephone systems? They are in effect being told to permit these people to use part of their lines and

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
systems so that people can rent their long distance charges.
Why does the member suppose the government has fallen off its very clear ownership set of principles in this case? Does it simply hate government-owned and provincially owned monopolies so badly that it is willing to close its eyes to that principle?

Mr. Speaker, I think it is a very interesting question. One has to wonder whether the member did not give the answer himself in posing the question in that what we have seen over the past eight and a half years has been a government interested in privatizing everything, whether it be Canada Post, Petro-Canada, Air Canada or almost anything we want to name. It has tried to take away and denationalize everything and put it out into the private sector.
Dealing with intellectual property, it seems that the agenda has been somewhat controlled by large transnational corporations such as AT&T. Is this another situation like that of the drug patent bill where the large transnational drug corporations wanted to ensure and assure their profits for a longer period of time. Similarly, do the AT&Ts of the telecommunications world want to get their fingers on to a pulse which they see as being more lucrative and more profitable?
I would suggest to the member for Mackenzie that this is a projection of the policies we have seen of this government to break the backs of the small Canadian companies and allow the AT&Ts of this world ample access to the telecommunications network of Canada, including the research and development aspect of it.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Nicole Roy-Arcelin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to tell you first of all that I will share my time with the hon. member for York-Simcoe.
Canada's history illustrates the importance of communications as a means and condition for the nation's economic, social and cultural development. In fact, telecommunications is the first Canadian high-technology industry and provides an essential infrastructure for the economic development of the country.
Canada now has three main communications systems, those of Stentor, Unitel and Telesat Canada; two mobile cellular telephone systems; one overseas telecommunications system, Teleglobe Canada; 49 other telephone companies, located mainly in Quebec and Ontario; about 200 radio communication companies providing mobile radio-telephone and paging services; and finally more than 22 companies specializing in the resale of services.
The whole industry-that is, the above companies as well as the equipment manufacturers-does $23 billion of business and employs over 100,000 people and is one of the fastest growing sectors of the Canadian economy. More than 98 per cent of Canadian households have a telephone and public surveys invariably show satisfaction with the quality of service. The telecommunications industry has grown essentially in a monopolistic framework. The telecommunications company had a monopoly and provided all the facilities, services and equipment, from sophisticated transmission and switching facilities which were the very base of its system to the ordinary residential or business telephone set.
However, regulation by the various governments was extremely fragmented. It was based on a series of different regimes involving only one level of government: seven provinces regulated 30 per cent of the Canadian market, while the federal agency regulated the rest. Thus major interprovincial trade barriers made the Canadian market smaller and more fragmented than it should have been.
A decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in August 1989 clarified and simplified the sharing of jurisdiction. The court concluded that the main telecommunications companies in Canada, namely telephone companies in the Stentor system, come under federal jurisdiction. This ruling thus paved the way to an open Canadian market.
In the past few years, we saw the emergence of a very complex technological and economic environment contributing to the gradual elimination of traditional boundaries between telecommunications markets thus calling into question the traditional monopolistic approach.
The diversity within the Canadian telecommunications market, together with the requirements of globalization and stiffening international competition, made inevitable a re-evaluation of government policy and regulatory practices.
April 19, 1993

I would first like to say that the present world trend in telecommunications is toward gradual liberalization of market regulation and privatization of state owned telecommunications companies.
In keeping with this trend and given the small size of our domestic market compared to the markets of our main trading partners and the complex fragmented regulatory structure, the Canadian government thought that the country needed a policy that could apply to the whole territory and a more flexible regulatory regime that could encourage innovation and the faster development of our leading high-tech industry.
The foundation of this policy was laid in 1987 and is the framework for Bill C-62.
The CRTC's recent decision to allow competition in the long-distance market makes new telecommunications legislation even more necessary.

In conclusion, pursuant to Standing Order 26(1) I move:
That the House continue to sit beyond the normal hour of
adjournment for the purpose of continuing consideration of Bill
C-62, an act respecting telecommunications.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-62 at second reading.
Canada today faces many great challenges. Technology and global economic forces are exerting a pervasive influence on all aspects of our lives. They are changing the nature of the goods and services we produce and the markets in which they are sold.
Globalization is also affecting the kind of jobs we have and the way we make a living. To an increasing degree the goods and services we produce are exported and the companies and workers we compete with are in foreign countries. These global economic and technological forces are making every country look more to trade for economic growth and the creation of new sources of wealth and jobs.
We can no longer afford to depend solely on our resource industries to carve out a place for ourselves in the new world economy. In the decades ahead we will
Government Orders
have to depend on our educational institutions, our highly skilled work force, our creativity and our ability to innovate to ensure that we continue to grow and prosper.
Telecommunications now plays a central role in many of these global economic and technological developments. We cannot hope to compete in the world information economy of the nineties and beyond without a strong telecommunications industry and a modem and efficient telecommunications infrastructure.
A critical step in this process is to update our outmoded telecommunications legislation and streamline the regulatory and policy making processes. The Railway Act, the principal statute by which the telecommunications industry is currently regulated, was enacted some 84 years ago in 1908 long before the computer, the microchip, the satellite, the optical fibre or the laser were invented. This gives you an idea why Bill C-62 is so important to all Canadians.
Bill C-62 provides a comprehensive legislative and regulatory framework for telecommunications that will ensure Canada keeps abreast of improvements in productivity and industrial competitiveness in the future.
This legislation will provide the industry with a more modem and efficient regulatory process by establishing a single, national legislative framework. The bill will streamline the regulatory process by giving the CRTC an important new tool, the power to forbear from regulating services which are subject to fair and equitable competition and is in the public interest. It will also provide a power to issue directions to the CRTC on general policy matters to support and enhance the principles laid out in the telecommunications policy objectives.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of my constituents in Sudbury to discuss proposed legislation and to scrutinize it on behalf of all Canadians.
Bill C-62 is an important bill. New telecommunications legislation is absolutely essential and has been needed for some time. It is also extremely important this legislation be done right because it has taken a very long time for it to come forward. We certainly do not want it to be handled in a willy-nilly fashion in order to push it through this place without it being appropriate.
As the 21st century approaches, Canadians find themselves in a world changing more rapidly than ever before. Global competition is upon us. We realize that successful nations in the years ahead will be those that understand and take advantage of the changes taking place.
The rapid growth of international trade and capital flows have created the so-called borderless world and Canada must find ways to ensure it is a winner in this new global economy. For this reason we on this side of the House will continue pursuing policies of reform here at home, reforms that will make Canada stronger, more united, and more competitive around the world.
The changes in the world economy are nowhere better reflected than in today's changing telecommunications industry. Global networks and players are changing the telecommunications universe and reinforcing the idea of a global village. If communications created the global village then telecommunications today is shrinking the global village.
Not only is this industry's own structure evolving, it is also playing many new roles. New technology, new protocols and new services are letting individuals and corporations use telecommunications services more and more often, whether it is a fax machine, automated bank teller, toll free phone call or computer sharing information on a network. Small, medium and large corporations use telecommunications to link offices, reach customers, and move billions of dollars of capital around the world daily on an instantaneous basis.
In short the age of our telecommunications system serving for simple phone calls is over. It has become an important building block in Canada's competitiveness and the unifying communications link among Canadians from coast to coast to coast.
The telecommunications sector is an essential tool for building vital economic and social links, marshalling industry, social, educational and cultural forces into an efficient national system of communication among Canadians of all regions.
April 19, 1993

Telecommunications can boost the competitive position of industries in all regions by making it possible to locate knowledge-intensive and service sector enterprises of the future in all parts of Canada. It is especially important in a country such as ours which is far-flung. Some communities are looking for ways of participating in the 21st century.
Let us look at what we are seeing today in BUI C-62. It appears as if the minister would like the House to deal swiftly with the bill which he introduced over a year ago on February 27, 1992 and which he is only at this time advancing for second reading.
We in the Liberal Party have supported this bUl going to committee but we said at the outset we wanted assurances that the minister planned changes to the bill as virtually everyone in the telecommunications industry has said are necessary. Until today and for 14 months that has not been forthcoming.
I wonder why the minister has not made some amendments to this bill. We are all very much aware they are needed, as is everyone in the industry. I have very little understanding why absolutely no changes were made to this proposed legislation.
We have some serious problems with the fact that the minister and his government have delayed this bill, not the opposition. The minister has had the tools at his disposal for over a year to build a national consensus on this bill and he has not done it.
The minister has had a very useful senate pre-study report in his hands since June 1992 and has failed to act on it. The minister has faded after 14 months to undertake a serious constructive effort that would have built a consensus on this bill and enabled it to come forward in a way that would have been good for the telecommunications industry, Canadian business and Canadians. That is how I see this process.
It should be a constructive open process and not one of delay. I want the record to clearly show that the government controls the agenda in this House. The opposition does not. Let the responsibility for this bUl
Government Orders
languishing on the back burner be on the minister's shoulders.
I certainly hope we do not start hearing outside this place that somehow the opposition has been responsible for the mishandling and delay of this bUl. The minister was unwUling to bring it forward. I want that to be absolutely clear.
We take telecommunications issues just as seriously as we do the parliamentary process. We are not a rubber stamp here to approve a flawed bill. It is not the opposition but the minister who is responsible for coming in at the eleventh hour with his bill asking us to trust him on the amendments. It becomes very difficult for anyone to support a bill going to committee when the minister himself raises questions about it.
Having said that, we put the interests of Canada above the minister's messy handling of this bill and we want it to go to committee. Why is this bill important?
Let me address for a moment why this bill is important. Telecommunications is Canada's electronic railroad for the 1990s. It employs more than 100,000 Canadians and generates over $20 billion in revenues. It has emerged as an important and strategic industry for our entire economy.
The bill can help us create the knowledge and intensive high technology jobs of the future. It can help Canada locate these jobs where people are, which is often outside traditional business centres and particularly in our regions.
All this cannot happen by itself. As an industry that remains highly regulated, the telecommunications sector requires the appropriate policy, legislative and regulatory environment in which to succeed. This is why Bill C-62 with proper amendments and improvements is a fundamentally important bill. It is also why we are so disappointed that it took nine years for the government to produce this bill and almost another full year before getting to second reading.
These delays say a great deal about the Conservative commitment to telecommunications. The delays and inaction going back to 1984 were not only poor public policy choices at the time but over time have contributed

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
to a closed door, behind the scenes decision-making process that in the end led us to a flawed bill.
In addition to these flaws, the government's failure to lead a national discussion of telecommunications policy means Canada has never developed a clear strategy. This government never sat down, looked at the telecommunications industry, studied all of its various component parts, compared how they worked together and came up with some clear directions.
That is the approach that should have taken place. It is a view that was supported by a number of witnesses to the Senate pre-study hearings on this bill. In our view, once a strategy was developed the government opposite could have taken directions from that for drafting a bill. Unfortunately we are now stuck with the results.
We have no national strategy but we have a flawed bill that needs a lot of work. Never was there a white paper, a green paper, any coloured paper or any thorough public review of telecom issues. Never did this government ask the people of Canada: "What are your goals? What do you want to see from your telephone system?"
Never over the past nine years did we see an open process that said to the business community: "Come and have your say. Let us put your comments on the record before we draft a bill, not after".
The worst part is that despite glowing words from Conservative ministers, from the Minister for International Trade and the hon. member for Frontenac to Flora MacDonald and the Minister of Communications, they have never produced the vision to match the rhetoric.
Let us briefly review these commitments. We can go as far back as the trade minister's November 1984 economic statement when he said: "There is a clear need for national telecommunications policy to take advantage of the opportunities presented by rapidly advancing technology and the growing demand by Canadians for new telecommunications services". He added: "Through regulatory reform the government can spur innovation and provide a major stimulus to the Canadian economy". Yet there was never a bold strategy leading to this Bill C-62.
I can keep going back but I will not because it just repeats itself and we will see over and over the lack of strategy and over-all planning that has gone into producing this bill.
Our present minister tabled Bill C-62 in February 1992. Four months later he said at a Senate pre-study: "To delay its implementation", and he was referring to Bill C-62, "would be to slow the growth of an industry which is vital to the Canadian economy".
Yet it is over a year after introduction and this bill is only now coming forward for second reading in the House of Commons. Canadians can see that this government has left this industry in a substantial policy vacuum while pillars of the sector were developing extremely quickly. The government simply never kept up with the pace of changes. It never addressed how the environment was progressing and therefore never demonstrated a clear understanding of what needed to be done. That is why we have a flawed bill before this House today.
In essence this government left Canada labouring under century old legislation and a long series of ad hoc decisions affecting the pillars of this industry, the onset of competition, the privatization of Telesat and Teleglobe, and tremendous advances in technology and services, with no coherent or co-ordinated approach from government, something we have called on this government to produce for years.
What are we left with in Bill C-62? What should the goals of this bill be? The bill must provide a fresh direction to the telecommunications sector so that it can maximize the benefits to every Canadian of the worldwide information revolution in terms of learning and literacy, education, training and communicating. It must bring the marvels of this revolution from our biggest cities to our outermost communities. However this bill, as introduced last February, is far from what the country needs.
Let me turn to a number of issues raised in the bill, just some of the issues raised in the Senate's report because we cannot address them all today. Let me deal first with how the bill addresses jurisdiction.
We support the bill's attempt to unify national jurisdiction over telecommunications. We supported the Supreme Court in August 1989 when it ruled in the AGT case largely in favour of federal jurisdiction over telecommunications.
Liberals believe Canada needs harmonized rules and regulations governing this sector if all Canadians are to have equal access to the benefits of the information revolution. How the transition rules work and how regional sensitivities are taken into account certainly must be studied at committee.
April 19, 1993

Clause 2 concerns definitions. In terms of definitions there was much study in the Senate on this question. I believe it is worth examining more closely how resellers are treated in this bill in terms of whether they should be included in the bill but then be considered for relief from the act where appropriate through either the exemption or the forbearance provisions. That must be explored.
We also need to see how the so-called hybrid companies will be dealt with. They are companies that may be part reseller but own some facilities and are therefore part carrier. This too must be cleared up at committee. As the CRTC said in the Senate the ambiguity in the definition must be removed by clearly setting out what is meant to be included and excluded.
As for power of direction, the government did establish a power of direction providing for broad policy directives to be issued by the Governor in Council as guidance to the CRTC in the Broadcasting Act. Having that in this bill for telecommunications matters is not a surprise. It raises a red flag of concern when the minister is establishing this new power of direction in telecom matters and maintaining the power to vary or rescind CRTC decisions at the same time. We do not want the CRTC becoming a rubber stamp for the minister if he has so much control over the process. That is our concern.
The question of exemptions from the act must be examined very closely. I agree with the Senate report that the CRTC should deal with exemptions when they come up. I am not convinced that specific exemptions for certain classes of carriers should be in the bill itself. If certain classes of carriers are worthy of exemption then the CRTC can certainly deal with this appropriately. Why do they have to be permanently in this bill?
On provincial consultation, in this transition to uniform national regulation of telecommunications, because of the Supreme Court's 1989 AGT ruling, it would be useful to have a mechanism for regional input. However, clause 14 dealing with provincial consultation must not create an open-ended, almost veto power over federal decisions that would inhibit an effective national telecommunications policy from working. Exactly what limits are appropriate under this clause must be carefully examined at committee.
Government Orders
Under clauses 17 and 23 concerning the minister's licensing of carriers, I have great difficulty with the minister grabbing so many new powers in this bill, in particular his idea of licensing carriers. First, we have never been convinced of the benefits of licensing at the same time that the CRTC is regulating communications carriers. The question is: Why politicize entry into this market? Why give the power to issue, renew and revoke licences if the licence in the minister's opinion furthers the bill's telecom objectives for Canada when the CRTC would still have to do the regulating anyway? It adds a layer of red tape that is not helpful and places the minister in the middle of a process that should be left up to the CRTC.
Again these straightforward arguments would have been clear to the government had it bothered to undertake an open public dialogue on these issues long before depositing a bill before Parliament. They are heavily supported by a number of interventions at the Senate hearings on Bill C-62. The suggestion to remove licensing altogether or to move it to the CRTC requires further attention.
What are extremely important are our Canadian ownership rules. If the minister is set to remove licensing from this bill then we will need to see how the criteria and objectives of the licensing regime will be met. Canadian ownership and control is one of the key areas. We believe we need to do everything we can to foster a strong, dynamic Canadian telecommunications system. We need to make sure our own people, our own workers, our researchers and scientists, our own manufacturers, software and hardware designers, all have a chance to prosper and remain on the leading edge of technology.
Putting Canada first is not the right way to put it, nor is closing the door to having Canada telcos participate in global alliances. We cannot stand in the way or stop globalization. What we say is let us make sure there are sufficient safeguards in place so that Canadian interests are protected so that when foreign companies come net benefits to Canada are top priority.
Security will definitely have to be paid to have the 80 per cent domestic ownership requirements work, how the grandfathering will work and how future ownership changes of any other company fits these new rules. We have to ensure that this bill serves Canadians and the Canadian telecommunications industry. It is absolutely

April 19, 1993
Government Orders
essential that this be the best possible bill we can put forward to serve the future needs of Canadians.
